goodAgainst.note: Vel'Koz is an immobile magic-damage artillery mage, so Galio's passive magic shield and Shield of Durand's damage reduction blunt much of his poke. Taking damage does not increase Galio's passive damage; close only after avoiding the knockback that can interrupt Justice Punch.

Ziggs deals mostly magic damage, which Galio's passive shield and Shield of Durand handle well, but his spells do not grant Galio more magic resist or passive damage. Match his waveclear, then roam when he stays behind the wave; save Justice Punch until Explosive Charge cannot knock you away.

Katarina must blink into Galio's control range to collect Daggers, whose pickup sharply reduces Shunpo's current cooldown. Shield of Durand's taunt interrupts Death Lotus and delays the next blink, so hold it for her committed channel rather than describing the Dagger itself as resetting.
Fizz is slippery, but he has to land on you to deal damage, and that landing is exactly when your taunt catches him, while your magic resist blunts the burst he does get off.
A magic-damage assassin into the champion built to stop her: your shield absorbs her burst, and the taunt is an area lock that catches her even around the shroud she relies on.

weakAgainst.note: Irelia can dash around minions before Shield of Durand finishes charging and sidestep the straight line of Justice Punch. Her sustained physical damage also bypasses the anti-magic defenses that make Galio durable in other lanes.
The lane is a race you have to win early: once his ultimate is online his blink dodges your taunt on reaction, his magic shield absorbs your Q, and he out-scales you from there.
Swain out-sustains the one thing your kit lacks, the damage to finish: his drain heals through your Q faster than you chip it off, and long brawls only pull his sustain further ahead.

Ryze clears quickly and can deny the priority Galio needs to roam. Spell Flux into Rune Prison roots Galio as he tries to engage, and Ryze's movement-speed proc helps him kite; Ryze does not have a native shield in his current Wild Rift kit.

Jayce's Cannon poke and Hyper Charge attacks are physical, but Lightning Field, Thundering Blow, and both stance-change attacks add magic damage. Galio's magic shield is not useless, yet it does not answer the long-range physical Shock Blast that controls the lane.

gamePlan.overview:
Galio is a tanky mid laner built to shut down magic damage. His empowered Colossal Smash attack gains damage from bonus magic resist, while Shield of Durand supplies a periodically refreshed magic-damage shield and damage reduction during its charge. Taking enemy spells does not grant Galio more magic resist or increase Colossal Smash. He is a roaming anti-mage control tank who clears the wave, reinforces fights, and locks down enemies who enter his range.

Galio wins through map pressure, not lane kills. Hero's Entrance targets an allied champion within its long but limited range, grants Galio's passive magic shield to allies around the chosen landing area, then sends Galio to that fixed location after a channel. The landing damages and knocks enemies back rather than knocking them up. In practice you clear the wave, win priority, and watch for fights within range. Winds of War chips and clears, Shield of Durand taunts nearby champions after its charge, and Justice Punch knocks enemies up along its straight dash.

His core weakness is that his damage is slow and his lockdown is committal. Shield of Durand must charge around Galio, while Justice Punch steps backward before dashing in a straight line, so mobile enemies can leave the taunt radius or sidestep the dash. Mobile mages who out-range him and dash-heavy skirmishers who refuse to stand in his kit are the lanes where his durability stops mattering.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Early lane is about using Galio's anti-magic defenses to preserve health and create priority. Push caster minions with Winds of War and chip the enemy mage, then let the passive magic shield refresh after a quiet window; enemy poke does not add damage to Colossal Smash. You are hunting priority more than a level-three solo kill: shove, force them to react, and start watching the river and side lanes. Against burst assassins, hold Shield of Durand for their commitment instead of spending it on cooldown.
gamePlan.midGame: Mid game is where Galio starts playing the whole map. Once your ultimate is up, every grouped fight elsewhere is one you can join: watch the side lanes and your jungler, and when a skirmish starts over scuttle or a dive looks live, channel Hero's Entrance and flip the numbers. Shove your wave first so mid tower stays safe while you travel, then make the roam count. Around dragon and herald, hold mid priority and arrive late and decisive, taunting their key target while your team collapses on the rest. A Galio with ult up and a shoved wave is rarely actually in his lane, and that is the whole point.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game Galio is a utility frontline with a knock-up, area taunt, and long-range reinforcement ultimate. You will not delete carries one on one, so stop trying. Your value is being durable enough to dive their back line or peel your own, then live through the focus while your team does the killing. Build against whatever damage type is hurting you, save Hero's Entrance for a fight within range, and use Winds of War and Shield of Durand to zone and peel.
gamePlan.teamfights: In teamfights Galio is the lockdown and the reinforcement at once. Use Hero's Entrance on an allied diver or threatened carry within range: allies around the selected area receive the magic shield immediately, and Galio lands at the location chosen when he cast it, damaging and knocking nearby enemies back. After landing, charge Shield of Durand to taunt nearby champions. If Galio starts in the fight, Justice Punch supplies the knockup and Shield of Durand supplies the taunt; W itself never knocks enemies up. Do not expect the landing point to follow a moving ally.

goodAgainst.note: Sion is a free poke target: too slow to reach the yordle, easy to hop away from when the charged knockup comes, and his slow engage loses to your faster wall-toss in fights.

Boomerang Throw and Hyper let Mini Gnar damage Garen without entering Judgment, while Hop preserves the distance after Decisive Strike begins. Boomerang Throw slows Mundo before he can remain in cleaver range, and repeated Hyper procs punish the maximum health his build adds. Keep Hop for the Infected Bonesaw slow or jungle pressure, kite in Mini Gnar instead of forcing a Mega Gnar brawl, and use the wave lead before Mundo's regeneration has enough items to erase the poke.

Camille's hookshot reaches the yordle and her true damage hurts squishy Mini form badly, while her adaptive shield blunts your poke trades.

Malphite does not care which Gnar he is hitting: armor blunts your boomerang poke, his Q chips you through the hops, and his ultimate covers so much ground that even Mini form struggles to sidestep it.

gamePlan.overview:
Gnar is two champions sharing a rage meter. Mini Gnar is a ranged yordle with boomerangs, bouncing hops, and enough movement speed to frustrate melee laners. At maximum Rage his abilities switch to their Mega versions for four seconds; casting one transforms him immediately, otherwise he transforms automatically. Mega Gnar's ultimate knocks nearby enemies in a chosen direction and only stuns those who collide with terrain.

The rage bar determines which fights Gnar can take. It fills as he fights and transforms him whether the timing suits him or not, so plan the wave and rotation around it: poke as Mini while the bar builds, then arrive as Mega becomes available. Mega Gnar needs a wall and a follow-up angle to create a strong engage, while Mini Gnar is vulnerable if the enemy starts before he can transform.

Against immobile melee, Gnar can pressure last-hits while preserving Hop for the opponent's approach. Gap closers and longer-range poke make that spacing harder and can force an early transformation or retreat.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Poke when the opponent walks up to farm, but avoid hitting the whole wave unless you want it to push. Catch Boomerang Throw when the route is safe for its cooldown refund, and preserve Hop against champions whose gap closer starts the all-in. Track Rage before trading: approaching transformation near a wall can create a stun sequence, while transforming during a retreat removes Mini Gnar's range and speed. Use the brief post-transformation exhaustion window to reset the wave rather than forcing another fight without Mega form available.
gamePlan.midGame: Fights now revolve around arrival timing and form. Before the six-minute objectives, crash the wave while building Rage so Mega Gnar is available near Herald. Herald is usually the stronger even trade, while a team built for grouped fighting can use Mega Gnar to start a dragon-soul plan. Approach the pit near terrain and look for a GNAR! angle that stuns several champions, but do not transform too early while clearing the last wave. If Rage is low, communicate it and poke safely until the engage is ready.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game, manage Rage and the side wave together. Arrive before Baron or Elder with enough nearby targets to prepare Mega form without transforming long before the contest. At maximum Rage, cast a Mega ability to transform immediately or account for the short automatic delay. When Mega is unavailable, kite with Hyper and Boomerang Throw instead of face-checking for an engage. Tell your team whether you can start the fight now or need time to rebuild.
gamePlan.teamfights: The ideal setup is Mini Gnar near maximum Rage or a fresh Mega Gnar with enemies beside terrain. Transform at the chosen moment, use Hop or Crunch to enter, and knock priority targets into a wall with GNAR! for the stun. Rage depletes throughout Mega form, so do not wait until the transformation is nearly over to engage. If the wall angle never appears, use the ultimate's displacement to peel or separate the frontline. In Mini form, attack from range and keep Hop available rather than entering fog first.

startingItem.name: Ruby Crystal
startingItem.note: Early health. His passive regenerates a share of missing health, so a bigger bar means faster recovery between trades.

boots.name: Armored Advance
boots.note: Armor and health, which let him hold the lane through the poke that keeps his passive regeneration switched off.

coreItems.name: Black Cleaver
coreItems.note: His E hits the same target repeatedly, so the armor shred reaches full stacks almost instantly. The move speed toward champions also fixes his lack of a gap closer.

coreItems.name: Dead Man's Plate
coreItems.note: Momentum builds while he walks someone down and triggers on his Q, which is the swing that starts every kill.

coreItems.name: Spear of Shojin
coreItems.note: Ability haste brings his E and his silence back sooner, which is most of his damage and all of his lockdown.

coreItems.name: Force of Nature
coreItems.note: Build this into repeated magic damage. The movement speed helps Garen reach Decisive Strike range, while the magic resistance keeps him spinning after Courage's brief defensive window ends.

coreItems.name: Amaranth's Twinguard
coreItems.note: Build this when you are fighting in the middle of the enemy team and need both armor and magic resist. Courage covers Garen's initial entry, then Twinguard activates while Judgment keeps him in combat.

situationalItems.name: Serpent's Fang
situationalItems.note: Build this when enemy shields absorb the damage Garen needs before Demacian Justice becomes lethal. His ultimate is missing-health-scaled true damage, not a fixed-threshold execution.

situationalItems.name: Thornmail
situationalItems.note: Build this against healing his E cannot out-damage. The Grievous Wounds applies from his own damage as well as when they attack him, so the spin keeps it applied.

situationalItems.name: Chainlaced Crushers
situationalItems.note: Boot swap against heavy magic damage and crowd control, which is what keeps him from reaching the person he silenced.

situationalItems.name: Divine Sunderer
situationalItems.note: The max health damage and heal both trigger on the attack his Q empowers, which turns a losing duel against a tank around.

situationalItems.name: Mercurial Scimitar
situationalItems.note: Build this when a root or stun keeps Garen outside silence and Judgment range. Cleansing it lets his movement speed and tenacity carry him through the rest of the approach.

keystoneRune.name: Conqueror
keystoneRune.desc: Gain stacks by damaging enemy champions. At maximum stacks, gain bonus damage and healing.
keystoneRune.note: His E hits the same target several times, so he stacks quickly and the healing adds to his passive regeneration.

primaryRunes.name: Demolish
primaryRunes.desc: Charge up a powerful attack against turrets.
primaryRunes.note: He shoves waves easily and his silence keeps a laner off him, so a won trade turns into tower damage.

primaryRunes.name: Second Wind
primaryRunes.desc: After taking damage from a champion, regenerate health over time.
primaryRunes.note: His passive regen only starts once he stops taking damage, and this covers the stretch before it kicks in.

primaryRunes.name: Overgrowth
primaryRunes.desc: Gain permanent maximum health when nearby minions or monsters die.
primaryRunes.note: He wants to walk at people through their damage, and the pool is what makes that walk survivable.

secondaryRunes.name: Nimbus Cloak
secondaryRunes.desc: After casting a summoner spell, gain movement speed and slow resistance.
secondaryRunes.note: Casting a summoner spell triggers movement speed and slow resistance, helping Garen deliver Decisive Strike before the target can kite his Judgment and ultimate range.

spells.name: Flash
spells.note: Must take. Essential for repositioning, escapes, and aggressive combos.

goodAgainst.note: Windwall blocks nothing you do: your silence cuts his dash chain mid-combo, your spin chews through his shield, and his only real window is when both your cooldowns are down.

Decisive Strike's silence briefly prevents Irelia from casting another dash or stun, but it does not remove her marks or resets. Time the silence during her committed dash chain, then keep Judgment on her as she moves through the wave.
Your silence catches him mid-pattern and puts his pull, dashes, and wall slam on hold, and his early levels are weak before he stacks resistances.
Landing the silence before Counter Strike goes up shuts down his whole dodge-and-stun plan, and his early levels cannot answer your kit; he only becomes a real duelist once he scales.

weakAgainst.note: Darius's bleed keeps Perseverance disabled, and Apprehend pulls Garen back when he tries to disengage. Crowd control does not cancel Judgment, but the displacement keeps Garen in range for Darius to build Hemorrhage stacks and threaten Noxian Guillotine.
Camille wins extended trades with true damage and a shield tuned against you, her wall dash escapes the all-in your kit depends on, and she only gets stronger with items.

She farms at a range your kit cannot reach and scales into a carry your missing-health finisher arrives too late to stop. Demacian Justice has no automatic execution threshold, so Kayle can still survive if its calculated true damage is not lethal.

Riposte can prevent Decisive Strike's damage and silence, but silence is not an immobilizing effect and therefore does not make Riposte stun Garen by itself. Fiora's max-health true-damage Vitals also outscale Garen in the side-lane duel.

Tumble keeps Vayne outside Judgment, Condemn interrupts Garen's straight-line Decisive Strike approach, and Silver Bolts bypass the armor and health he normally relies on. Keep the wave near your turret, wait for Tumble or Condemn to be spent, and use brush or Flash to shorten the approach rather than running at her through open lane.

gamePlan.overview:
Garen is one of the simplest and most reliable Baron laners: easy to learn and solid enough to climb with forever. His passive regenerates back any trade that does not kill him, his empowered strike silences, his spin shreds armor, and his ultimate deals true damage that scales with the target's missing health. It is a powerful finisher, not a fixed-threshold execution.

The trade pattern is simple and repeatable: walk up with the speed from Decisive Strike, silence so they cannot answer, spin through them, and walk away while your passive heals the cost. No mana, no resource bar, no skillshots to miss. Combo champions hate the silence; attrition champions hate the regen.

What Garen cannot do is force anyone to fight him. He has no real gap closer, so disciplined ranged opponents and kiting teams leave him with nothing to hit. He wins by punishing mistakes in lane and finishing low-health targets late.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Farm the first couple of levels and let your regen top you off between waves. Once your kit is online, the short trade is yours whenever you want it: Q for the speed and silence, spin, and leave before their answer comes back up. The silence is the whole trick, since it locks out counterplay for exactly the window you need. In ranged matchups, do not chase a poke war you cannot win. Sit at the edge of experience range, regen, and punish the one time they step too far forward.
gamePlan.midGame: After completing the first fighting item, crash the Baron wave before moving toward Herald. Approach from fog and use Decisive Strike to silence a reachable mid laner or jungler while allies are close enough to finish the target. Keep Courage available for the return crowd control and avoid chasing beyond your team, since Garen has no movement tool for the exit.
gamePlan.lateGame: Your job is to lock down and finish one target. Run at the squishiest enemy you can reach, silence them so they cannot flash or dash away, spin, and cast Demacian Justice only when its current missing-health-scaled damage will finish them. The resists from W and your items let you survive more of the dive than enemies expect. If their team kites well, peel instead: a silence on their diving assassin protects your carry almost as well as it kills theirs.
gamePlan.teamfights: Pick one victim before the fight starts, usually their most fragile damage dealer, and spend the whole fight getting next to them. Enter after the enemy's first round of cooldowns, silence, spin, and hold your ultimate until its true damage is lethal instead of using it as poke. If you cannot walk in through the front, wait at the flank. A Garen who arrives ten seconds late to the right target beats one who arrives instantly at the wrong one.

startingItem.name: Ruby Crystal
startingItem.note: Early health, which is the stat his whole scaling plan is built on.

boots.name: Armored Advance
boots.note: Armor and health for surviving the lane long enough to start stacking his ultimate.

coreItems.name: Heartsteel
coreItems.note: His ultimate already gives permanent health per kill, so this stacks health from a second source at the same time.

coreItems.name: Hollow Radiance
coreItems.note: Magic resistance plus a burn on everything standing near him, and the middle of the fight is where he already is. It clears waves while he does it.

coreItems.name: Unending Despair
coreItems.note: Heals him off the damage he takes, which pays out in exactly the long fights he wants. The longer he holds the middle of their team, the more it gives back.

coreItems.name: Thornmail
coreItems.note: Build this against healing. The Grievous Wounds applies from your own damage as well as when they attack you, so his area damage spreads it across a group.

coreItems.name: Amaranth's Twinguard
coreItems.note: Build this when you are fighting in the middle of the enemy team and need both armor and magic resist. Cho'Gath's Feast health makes each point of Twinguard resistance more valuable while he walks through the frontline.

situationalItems.name: Sunfire Aegis
situationalItems.note: Build this instead of Hollow Radiance when the enemy damage is mostly physical, since it trades the magic resistance for armor and keeps the burn.

situationalItems.name: Abyssal Mask
situationalItems.note: Build this when the enemy has multiple AP threats and your team has magic damage worth amplifying, since it makes everyone standing near him take more of it.

situationalItems.name: Frozen Heart
situationalItems.note: Build this against attack speed carries. The aura slows their attacks for as long as he is next to them, which is most of a fight.

situationalItems.name: Hextech Rocketbelt
situationalItems.desc: AP engage item with a dash
situationalItems.note: Build this when you want ability power and a way to close into Feral Scream or Feast range after Rupture lands. Rupture itself is already ranged; Rocketbelt is for the follow-up, not for casting the knockup.

situationalItems.name: Chainlaced Crushers
situationalItems.note: Boot swap against heavy magic damage and crowd control. The tenacity is what gets him through the lockdown aimed at keeping him off the target he wants to Feast.

situationalItems.name: Force of Nature
situationalItems.note: Build this when the enemy team has two or more AP champions. The move speed also helps him close into silence range.

situationalItems.name: Kaenic Rookern
situationalItems.note: Build this against one large magic burst when Cho'Gath can reset between fights. The shield protects his approach into silence and Feast range, and his stacked health makes that anti-magic barrier larger.

situationalItems.name: Randuin's Omen
situationalItems.note: Build this when the enemy team has multiple crit champions. Cho'Gath has to walk into Feast range, and the crit reduction gives his large health pool more time to reach a carry and finish them with Feast's fixed true damage.

situationalItems.name: Mantle of the Twelfth Hour
situationalItems.note: The lifeline gives bonus max health when he drops low, which is a bigger swing on a champion already stacking it.

keystoneRune.name: Grasp of the Undying
keystoneRune.desc: Every 4 seconds in combat, your next attack against a champion deals bonus damage and heals you.
keystoneRune.note: Its health growth stacks on top of the permanent health his ultimate collects, so both point the same way.

primaryRunes.name: Demolish
primaryRunes.desc: Charge up a powerful attack against turrets.
primaryRunes.note: He shoves the wave with his silence cone and then takes the tower, which turns a stalled lane into a lead.

primaryRunes.name: Second Wind
primaryRunes.desc: After taking damage from a champion, regenerate health over time.
primaryRunes.note: Chip damage is what actually pushes him off the wave, and this regenerates it back between trades so he keeps farming.

primaryRunes.name: Overgrowth
primaryRunes.desc: Gain permanent maximum health when nearby minions or monsters die.
primaryRunes.note: His ultimate already stacks health, and this compounds a pool his whole kit scales with.

secondaryRunes.name: Axiom Arcanist
secondaryRunes.desc: Empower your spell-focused burst with extra damage and scaling for ability-heavy champions.
secondaryRunes.note: It amplifies his ultimate, so Feast hits harder, and a takedown refunds part of its remaining cooldown.

spells.name: Flash
spells.note: Must take. Essential for repositioning, escapes, and aggressive combos.

goodAgainst.note: A scaling contest he cannot actually win: his shield and health stack build toward a late game your Feast eats one true-damage bite at a time, and your sustain outlasts his chip damage.

Nasus wants quiet stacking and your lane refuses to allow it: Rupture and spikes punish every last hit he walks up for, your sustain shrugs off his early trades, and Feast means your late game arrives at least as strong as his.

Tryndamere wants to spin in, crit, and brawl, and your kit answers every step: the silence cuts his fury spending mid-trade, Rupture makes his engage a gamble, and your health pool outlasts his crit fishing. Only the undying window late deserves real respect.

A tank mirror where your half of the damage is magic and his armor stack answers none of it, while Feast's true damage keeps widening the health gap no matter what he builds. His ultimate is his only scary moment.

weakAgainst.note: Darius is the early bully you cannot ignore: his bleed out-damages Carnivore's refunds, the pull cancels your walk-away sustain game, and Noxian Guillotine's true damage grows with Hemorrhage rather than checking a fixed execute threshold. Your late game wins if you survive without feeding him full stacks.
Vitals scale off your huge health pool and her true damage ignores the armor you stack. She sidesteps Rupture, parries the silence you need to pin her, and wins any duel fought in her windows.

Gwen deals percent-health magic damage into a champion made almost entirely of health. While she is inside Hallowed Mist and Cho'Gath is outside it, she is unaffected by his attacks and abilities, so enter the mist or wait it out before committing Rupture, Feral Scream, or Feast.

Vayne is built to dismantle exactly what you are building: Silver Bolts take percent-health true damage out of your stack, Tumble slides around Rupture, and Condemn keeps you off her when you finally get close.

gamePlan.overview:
Cho'Gath is a tank who turns eating into a win condition. Carnivore restores both health and mana whenever he kills an enemy unit, with double recovery from champions, turrets, and epic monsters. Feast is the payoff: a bite of true damage that grows his size and maximum health whenever it kills its target. The longer the game runs, the bigger he gets, until the enemy is fighting a giant with more health than anyone else on the map.

The rest of the kit is reliable crowd control. Rupture flips enemies into the air on a delay, Feral Scream silences a cone so combo champions cannot finish their patterns, and Vorpal Spikes turn his attacks into waveclear that feeds his passive. He does not need kills to scale, just time and farm.

He struggles against anything that deals damage in percentages. He has no dash or gap closer, and his body only gets bigger and easier to hit, so kiting lanes and true damage duelists turn his size against him. Cho'Gath wins by surviving those lanes on sustain, landing the knockup that starts fights, and making the game last long enough for him to finish growing.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Eat first, fight later. Last-hit with Vorpal Spikes, let Carnivore refund the poke you soak, and treat the early levels as a farming exercise the enemy interrupts at their own risk. Rupture is your trade starter and your gank insurance: hold it for the moment they commit to a minion, or drop it behind you when their jungler shows. The silence wins any exchange against a champion who needs a combo to hurt you, so save it for their pattern rather than the wave. You do not need to win this lane. You just need to still be standing in it when Feast comes online.
gamePlan.midGame: Feast changes what the lane is about: every enemy recall lets you collect a growth stack from the wave, and every skirmish near you risks the bite. Start looking for the Rupture that flips a fight, especially in river fights where the knockup plus silence turns your team's follow-up into a kill. Stack Feast on whatever is safe when the map is quiet, and on champions when it is not. At objectives your job is simple: stand in the pit, be enormous, and make the enemy choose between hitting the dragon and being eaten next to it.
gamePlan.lateGame: You are the biggest thing on the map and the fight is shaped by that fact. Walk straight at their carries, Rupture the clump as your team engages, and silence whichever champion most needs their abilities to matter. Feast is a large fixed true-damage bite, not a fixed-health-threshold execution; when it kills the target, the resulting stack makes the next fight harder for them to win. Check for percent-health carries before you commit, because a Vayne or a Gwen treats your size as a damage bonus. Go in after they spend their answers, and finish whoever your knockup catches.
gamePlan.teamfights: Start the fight or ruin theirs. A hidden Rupture under the enemy backline is one of the best engages a tank can offer, and the silence stops the escape cast they want after the leap resolves. Stand where your carries need a wall, soak the engage that comes for them, and spend Feast when its displayed fixed true damage will kill a valuable target or safely earn a growth stack. You have no dash, so pick your position early and make the enemy fight around it.

startingItem.name: Amplifying Tome
startingItem.note: Early ability power strengthens the repeated Bountiful Harvest damage that does most of the work in his first clear, as well as Reap and Terrify against camps.

boots.name: Spellslinger's Shoes
boots.note: Magic penetration turns his ultimate from a scare into a kill before his items arrive.

coreItems.name: Malignance
coreItems.note: Ultimate haste means more Crowstorms per game, and the burn ticks on everyone standing in the crows.

coreItems.name: Blackfire Torch
coreItems.note: His ultimate and drain hit several enemies at once, so the stacking bonus counts multiple champions and stays near its cap.

coreItems.name: Rabadon's Deathcap
coreItems.note: Multiplies his ability power, and his crows tick for five full seconds, so it decides whether an ambush wipes a team.

coreItems.name: Zhonya's Hourglass
coreItems.note: Crowstorm keeps dealing damage during stasis, so he can blink into the enemy team, activate Zhonya's after they turn on him, and let the remaining storm ticks land safely. Buy Seeker's Armguard early for the armor and ability power.

coreItems.name: Void Staff
coreItems.note: Cuts the magic resist that lets enemies stand inside Crowstorm and survive its full channel. Choose it over Cryptbloom when heavy magic resistance makes maximum ultimate damage more valuable than haste and team healing.

situationalItems.name: Hextech Rocketbelt
situationalItems.desc: AP engage item with a dash
situationalItems.note: Build this when your ambushes start at the edge of a fight. The dash closes the last gap after his blink.

situationalItems.name: Morellonomicon
situationalItems.note: Build this when the enemy heals through his crows. Buy Oblivion Orb early, since the anti-heal works from the component and the full item can wait.

situationalItems.name: Oceanid's Trident
situationalItems.note: Build this when shields absorb Fiddlesticks's ambush. The first Crowstorm ticks reduce shields across the group before the remaining channel and allied follow-up land.

situationalItems.name: Rylai's Crystal Scepter
situationalItems.note: The slow keeps enemies inside the crows, which is the main problem with an ultimate they can walk out of.

situationalItems.name: Banshee's Veil
situationalItems.note: Build this when the enemy has crowd control ready for his channel, since interrupting the wind-up cancels the whole ultimate.

situationalItems.name: Liandry's Torment
situationalItems.note: His crows tick constantly, so the max health burn stays applied to the frontline standing in them.

situationalItems.name: Infinity Orb
situationalItems.note: Crits against low health targets, which finishes the ones his crows chipped down as they walked out.

situationalItems.name: Cryptbloom
situationalItems.note: The alternative to Void Staff. Less penetration, but the ability haste and healing on takedown help when his ambush opens a fight his team joins. Choose it when enemies have not built much magic resist, so trading Void Staff's extra damage for more ability haste and an area heal after takedowns is worthwhile.

keystoneRune.name: Ice Overlord
keystoneRune.desc: Immobilizing an enemy champion creates icy beams and a frozen zone that slows enemies inside.
keystoneRune.note: Crowstorm's opening fear immobilizes the group Fiddlesticks ambushes, creating the frozen zone and protective ice immediately. The extra Armor and Magic Resistance help this fragile mage survive after blinking into the enemy team, giving Crowstorm and Bountiful Harvest more time to deal their full damage.

primaryRunes.name: Axiom Arcanist
primaryRunes.desc: Empower your spell-focused burst with extra damage and scaling for ability-heavy champions.
primaryRunes.note: His ultimate is his entire champion, so a rune that amplifies it specifically is worth more to him than to almost anyone.

primaryRunes.name: Absolute Focus
primaryRunes.desc: While above 70% health, gain bonus adaptive force.
primaryRunes.note: He picks the fight from stealth at full health, so the bonus is active on the ultimate he opens with.

primaryRunes.name: Gathering Storm
primaryRunes.desc: Gain increasing adaptive force every few minutes as the game goes on.
primaryRunes.note: He is a scaling ambusher whose ultimate gets stronger with every item, so a rune that grows over the game fits.

secondaryRunes.name: Sudden Impact
secondaryRunes.desc: Deal bonus true damage after using mobility or exiting stealth.
secondaryRunes.note: His ultimate blinks him in, so the bonus true damage lands on the first tick of crows.

spells.name: Flash
spells.note: Must take. Essential for repositioning, escapes, and aggressive combos.

spells.name: Smite
spells.note: Required for Jungling. Secures objectives and sustains through camp clears.

goodAgainst.note: Shyvana wants to farm, but Dragon's Descent gives her hard displacement that can interrupt your channels. Track the ultimate before committing Crowstorm, then punish her limited control once it is spent.
Graves clears fast and bursts hard, but a fear from the brush turns his aggression into a free Drain, and he has no way out of it once he commits.
Nidalee wins the poke war but cannot kite a fear she walks into, and your Drain out-sustains her spear chip. Ambushes take away the range game she relies on.

weakAgainst.note: Lee Sin is online at level three while you are still working through your clear, and he can find you mid-Drain with a teammate. His strong window comes long before yours does.

Talon has no crowd control that interrupts Crowstorm, but his dash-in burst can kill your fragile frame during the channel before the ultimate goes off. Keep vision on his approach and channel from fog where he cannot reach you in time.

Olaf's Ragnarok makes him immune to the fear, silence, and slow your control relies on. Reap still damages him, but it cannot stop his approach, and his true damage shreds your squishy frame while you channel.

gamePlan.overview:
Fiddlesticks is a scaling ambush jungler who farms quietly, then turns a single brush into a fight the enemy cannot win. Bountiful Harvest drains several monsters at once to speed up his full clear, and the whole champion is built around one idea: stand still in a bush long enough and you become a fake ward that fears, silences, and blows up anyone who walks past.

He wins through scaling and ambush, not early aggression. His first clears are slow, so the plan is to get through the full clear and scuttle that put Crowstorm online, then farm toward his first item while he starts making picks. Crowstorm is the centerpiece: a blink into a storm of fear and damage, dropped from an unwarded flank bush. Once it is online, his ganks and objective setups stop being fair.

The catch is the early window, and good opponents know it. Through that first clear, before Crowstorm lands, he is slow, immobile, and squishy, with no way to fight off a jungler who finds him mid-camp. Anyone who invades him or catches him channeling Drain can end his game before it starts. He is terrifying when allowed to set up and helpless when he is not.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Your first clear is about staying alive, not racing. Start on a camp where Drain does the work, use Bountiful Harvest to hit several monsters at once, and accept that you are slower than the duelists across the map. Do not go looking for a gank before your ultimate. Take the full clear and the scuttle, which is what puts Crowstorm online, because guaranteed level five matters more than a low-pressure walk into lane.

Once it is up, the loop starts: clear, then use the camp respawn timer to find a flank where the storm lands on someone who cannot walk out of it. Scuttle itself is risky, since you can win the crab fight by fearing them off it but have no exit if an invader collapses on you, so take the safe crab and ward your jungle entrances. Track the enemy jungler and never drain a camp with no vision behind you.
gamePlan.midGame:
Crowstorm is strongest when an objective forces the enemy team into one cramped area. Set up before they commit rather than chasing them after. Sitting unseen in a river or pit bush turns you into a trap, and a fight that opens with a Terrified carry running the wrong way usually just ends, so contest whenever your ultimate is up. If it is down, take neither and farm, because Fiddlesticks without Crowstorm loses objective fights on stats alone.

In an even game Herald is the cleaner trade, since it turns into a tower without needing you to win a five on five, though a team that fights well is a reason to play for soul. Between objectives, clear a quadrant and hunt while the camps respawn, and pick your invades carefully, because getting caught deep without your ultimate hands the game back.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game is where Fiddlesticks controls the map. Every objective becomes a setup: park in a bush near Baron or dragon, let your team bait the contest, and drop Crowstorm when both sides collapse. You are the reason the enemy cannot start an objective without full vision and a flank check, and one missed sweep through your bush ends with their backline feared and silenced. The cooldown window is still the danger. If you ult into a bad fight or burn it as an escape, you spend the next stretch as a soft, slow body, so hold it for the fight that decides the objective rather than a small skirmish. One good Crowstorm can flip a game.
gamePlan.teamfights: This is the job you were built for. The ideal fight starts before the enemy knows there is one: you are already in a flank bush, unseen, watching them line up, and you blink Crowstorm into the middle of their team right as they commit. The storm fears several targets, the silence locks out their escapes and key spells, and the damage chews through their whole side while your team cleans up the panic. Aim for the cluster, not one hero, and land on their carries so the fear scatters the damage dealers. If you cannot flank, your fear and Drain still anchor a fight, but a Fiddlesticks who ambushes from the side is as close as the jungle gets to deleting a teamfight with one button.

startingItem.name: Long Sword
startingItem.note: Simple early attack damage. His passive also converts move speed into attack damage, so both halves of his scaling start early.

boots.name: Immortal Treads
boots.note: Move speed is not a throwaway stat on him. His passive turns bonus move speed directly into attack damage.

coreItems.name: Trinity Force
coreItems.note: Spellblade triggers on the empowered attack his E gives him, which speeds up his clear. The move speed also becomes damage through his passive.

coreItems.name: Manamune
coreItems.note: Turns his mana pool into attack damage, which matters because spamming his Q drains mana fast.

coreItems.name: Serylda's Grudge
coreItems.note: The slow keeps a target inside his Q radius, and the armor penetration keeps those repeated hits meaningful.

coreItems.name: Spear of Shojin
coreItems.note: Ability haste means more Q casts, which is his clear speed and the empowered follow-up his damage needs.

coreItems.name: Death's Dance
coreItems.note: Spreads burst damage out over a few seconds, which gives his W time to heal it back while he keeps fighting.

keystoneRune.name: Phase Rush

goodAgainst.note: Talon blinks in to burst and roll out, but Devastating Charge runs him down before his escape resets and Spirit of Dread heals through whatever he commits. A squishy assassin cannot kite your speed.
Kha'Zix needs a clean burst and reset, but he cannot kill a healthy bruiser who heals through his leap, and he cannot escape Devastating Charge afterward.
Warwick wants the long drain duel, but your Spirit of Dread out-heals his bite while your speed denies the chase his ultimate needs. You match his healing and beat his mobility.

weakAgainst.note: Jarvan's flag-and-drag and his ult arena are built to trap a momentum champion. He pins you mid-charge and walls you in, and your speed means nothing inside that box.

Nunu's snowball catches you mid-charge and stops the momentum your whole kit rides on, while his percent-health bite chunks you through the brawl. His body also blocks the angles you want to engage from.
Amumu's Bandage Toss and Curse of the Sad Mummy lock down the charge your whole game depends on, and his percent-health aura chips you through the brawl. The stun lands the moment you commit.

gamePlan.overview:
Hecarim is a momentum fighter: he gets faster the longer he runs and hits harder the faster he is moving. Rampage carves through camps while refunding its own cooldown, his passive turns bonus movement speed into bonus damage, and Devastating Charge ends a long run with a knockback. He does not sneak up on people; he outruns them.

In the jungle he is an early-to-mid tempo jungler who snowballs through ganks rather than farming to a late spike. Spirit of Dread keeps him standing through long skirmishes, while Onslaught of Shadows is the gank tool that defines him: a long-range dashing fear that catches flashes, starts dives, and lets him collapse on a lane from far away. The plan is to clear, find a kill once the rotation is done, and turn that lead into the next objective.

His core weakness is his identity. Take away the room he needs to build speed and you take away his damage and his threat. Slows, roots, and walls strand him mid-charge, and a team that wards the right brush sees the gank coming early. He wants chaos and open ground, and a disciplined, peel-heavy team can shut his engage down completely.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Your first clear is about arriving on time, not clearing as fast as possible. Start on a strong-side camp, max Rampage first, and keep its empowered follow-up active by hitting large monsters. Lean on Spirit of Dread through the bigger packs for defenses and healing, then path toward scuttle and level five.

From there you gank while the camps respawn. Come in from a wide angle so Devastating Charge has time to build speed before contact. Onslaught of Shadows fears and slows enemies around Hecarim when he arrives, making them flee away from him, so aim the landing point to send a target toward your laner rather than expecting them to remain in place. Use Devastating Charge for the follow-up knockback, then return to camps when the play ends.
gamePlan.midGame:
Onslaught of Shadows lets Hecarim reach and reshape an objective fight before a slower jungler. Be the one who arrives first and starts it: fear the enemy off the pit, knock their frontliner away from it, and let your team clean up the panic. Contest both when your team is ahead on early fights. In an even game take Herald, since the tower it buys does not depend on winning a five on five, and save the dragon priority for a team that genuinely wants soul.

Between objectives, take short clears and gank while the camps respawn, but never farm a full rotation while a lane is shoved and a kill is sitting there. Counter-jungling suits you because you can charge out of any bad spot the moment it sours.
gamePlan.lateGame: Hecarim does not fall off hard, but the game stops giving him free room to build speed. Scaled carries with peel and a front line that holds its shape can blunt the engage you relied on earlier, so your value shifts toward flanking and timing rather than face-first dives. Build enough speed and resists to survive the trip in, then use the long approach to your advantage: come from an angle their wards do not cover, and the fear plus knockback still scatters a backline that thought it was safe. Baron and Elder fights are where you matter most now, since a clean Onslaught of Shadows onto their grouped team can decide the objective before damage is even traded. Watch enemy crowd control cooldowns, because one well-timed root is the difference between a game-winning flank and a wasted body.
gamePlan.teamfights: Build movement speed from a side angle, then use Onslaught of Shadows when its fear can disrupt several enemies or separate a carry from peel. Devastating Charge can displace the selected target after the fear, while Spirit of Dread and Rampage sustain the follow-up. Track the crowd control that can stop Hecarim after he arrives and wait for allied follow-up before crossing the enemy formation. If the backline angle is covered, peel with the fear and displacement rather than forcing the flank.

gamePlan.overview:
Jarvan IV is the jungler who traps people. His flag plants a banner, his lance pulls him to it with a knockup, and his ultimate, Cataclysm, drops a ring of walls around his target. The whole kit is built to catch one enemy and leave them nowhere to go.

He clears at a decent pace and his gank is one of the most reliable in the role: plant the flag past the target, pull yourself through them for the knockup, and your laner finishes the job. He is an early-to-mid tempo bruiser who wants to be on the map constantly, turning small leads into towers, dragons, and the picks that open a Baron. He is not a farm-to-carry scaler or a stealthy assassin.

His weakness is the same combo that makes him scary. It is one dash on a real cooldown, and once it is spent he is a melee bruiser with no second way out. He locks down a single target hard but offers little once that target is handled, and good teams learn to bait the flip and punish the gap that follows.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Demacian Standard into Dragon Strike clears camps quickly, but the same combo also gives Jarvan one of the strongest early ganks in the roster. After your first three camps, check the nearest lanes and the enemy's likely second-buff route. Break the clear when a knockup will force Flash, secure a kill, or catch the opposing jungler with lane support; otherwise finish the camps and arrive at scuttle with Cataclysm close.

Place the flag beyond the target so Dragon Strike carries you through them, then slow with Golden Aegis while your laner follows. Weave an attack on each fresh target for Martial Cadence's current-health damage, since the flag-and-drag itself does not trigger the passive. Jarvan's early advantage comes from making the first reliable move, not from forcing every possible fight.
gamePlan.midGame:
Cataclysm gives Jarvan a decisive way to isolate the enemy jungler or a vulnerable carry near the first objectives. Place Demacian Standard across the dragon or Herald wall, then connect Dragon Strike to the flag to dash through and knock enemies up along Jarvan's path. The combo does not throw them toward your team, so your allies must already be in position to follow before you commit Cataclysm.

Between objectives, move between lanes and river with purpose instead of power-farming a full loop: any gank you land with a first item is a kill. Counter-jungle the slow scalers who cannot answer your engage, and set vision around the next objective before it spawns.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you stop being the carry and become the engage tool. Group with your team and hold flag-lance for the moment that matters. Across a Baron wall, the combo dashes Jarvan through and knocks enemies up in place; it does not fling them to his allies. Follow with Cataclysm only when the arena traps a valuable target without walling out your own team's damage.
gamePlan.teamfights: Pick your target before the fight starts, because your whole fight is one decision made well. The dream play is a flag-lance onto their most dangerous carry, then Cataclysm to wall them in while your team collapses on someone who cannot leave. Use the dash to cross terrain and reach the backline that thinks it is safe, and remember the ultimate walls can box out your own allies, so angle the arena to trap the enemy, not your follow-up. If you cannot reach the carry, the flip still works as peel: knock their diving assassin off your carry and back into your team. Once your engage is spent you are a frontline body, so soak what you can, but the kill you set up with the flip is what decides the fight.

Syndra zones divers with her scatter stun and orbs, but your wave resets weave through her spacing, and an immobile mage with no escape cannot survive you once the stun is spent.
Your dashes match his mobility and your sustain outlasts his short trades. His pole vault dodges one spell, not your reset chain, so his kill windows are brief while your pressure is constant.

Diana shields your opening trade and out-skirmishes you with her own resets in long fights. Her ultimate pulls you in, taking away the engage timing you usually control.
Every dash you make feeds her passive, and her fear punishes the exact mobility your kit runs on. She zones you off the wave and bursts you the moment you engage through it.
His windwall blocks the blades that set up your stun, his knockup interrupts your dash chain, and the extended duel you both want favors his shield and sustain.

gamePlan.overview:
Irelia is a melee skirmisher who uses the minion wave as a chain of dash targets. Bladesurge resets when its target dies and becomes available again almost immediately after hitting a target marked Unsteady. Her passive stacks attack speed, gaining bonus magic damage on attacks at four stacks. Defiant Dance reduces incoming damage but does not block crowd control, while Flawless Duet places two blades whose connecting line stuns and marks enemies hit.

In mid she plays for the snowball. She wants to win an early trade, take wave control, and turn that lead into resets. Vanguard's Edge marks champions hit by its initial barrage, then creates a blade wall around the first champion struck; enemies crossing that wall take magic damage and are heavily slowed once, but their defenses are not shredded. She deals sustained damage rather than one-shot burst.

The cost is a weak early game and hard counters to her mobility. Before her first item she is a melee champion with a thin health bar walking up into spells, and any point-and-click stun, taunt, or untargetable button shuts her dash chain down. She wins by surviving the poke, hitting her item spike, and never giving you a safe window again.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Accept that the first few levels are not yours. Last-hit at the edge of your range, take the poke you have to, and look for short trades: dash in, land your stun, and walk out with attack-speed stacks before they answer. Against ranged mids, do not force kills that are not there. Stay even and accept that walking up costs health you cannot get back yet. Track the enemy jungler before you commit a dash forward, because an Irelia who used Bladesurge on the wave has no escape, and every jungler knows it. Your job is to reach your first item even, then turn the lane your way.
gamePlan.midGame: Once your first item lands, the lane flips your way and the roams start. Shove the wave with your resets, then leave. You are a real roam threat, and a kill in a side lane is worth more than the minions you gave up. Your dash makes you great at contesting scuttle and joining fights your jungler starts, and mid priority lets you crash the wave and walk to dragon or herald with tempo. Keep the wave shoving when an objective is near so you arrive first, and use your stun to punish anyone caught too far up. This is where a snowball turns into pressure nobody can contain.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game Irelia deals sustained damage, so she needs to reach a carry and keep attacking rather than rely on one burst. Push a side lane between fights, then enter grouped fights only after identifying Bladesurge kills or Unsteady marks. Defiant Dance reduces incoming damage but will not carry Irelia through crowd control, so wait for the most dangerous disables before committing.
gamePlan.teamfights: Find an entry that leaves a marked unit available for repositioning. Land Vanguard's Edge on a reachable carry, use Bladesurge on the mark, and place Flawless Duet so its connecting line adds the stun and another reset. The ultimate wall damages and slows the first crossing rather than pinning targets to terrain. If the carry cannot be reached safely, damage the frontline while preserving a dash route instead of committing without a reset.

Sion is large and his charged Decimating Smash is telegraphed enough to dash aside. Defiant Dance reduces its damage but does not prevent the knockup, so reposition rather than treating W as crowd-control immunity.
Your dashes reach both forms, and W shrugs off the boomerang poke Mini Gnar relies on, so a stun into combo kills him before the rage bar saves him. Only Mega Gnar near a wall is a real threat.

Renekton's Fury-empowered Ruthless Predator locks Irelia down before Defiant Dance can reposition her, while Slice and Dice exits before she rebuilds Ionian Fervor. Do not contest the wave while his Fury bar is red, preserve Bladesurge targets behind you, and take longer trades only after the empowered stun and second dash are unavailable.

Armor answers your stacks, his poke is hard to dodge forever, and his engage covers too much ground to simply walk away from. His level 5 combo deletes squishies, and early Irelia qualifies, though you out-scale him later.

Counter Strike dodges the attacks that carry Ionian Fervor and then stuns Irelia at the end, so entering with a fully stacked passive does not solve the duel. Use Flawless Duet to force Counter Strike from range, dash away before it finishes, and commit through the wave only during that cooldown.

gamePlan.overview:
Irelia is a blade dancer whose dash resets on targets killed by Bladesurge and becomes available again almost immediately when it hits a target marked Unsteady. Her passive stacks attack speed as her abilities hit enemies, and at four stacks her attacks against champions and minions gain bonus magic damage; it does not stack attack damage.

Lane is her hardest stretch. Early Irelia hits soft, needs stacks to trade at all, and loses badly to bullies who break her pattern. Her job is to farm with the dash, survive the counterpicks, and reach the first item where her kit comes online.

When it does, she is one of the most oppressive skirmishers in the game. Her stun bridges the gap, her W shrugs off the spell meant to stop her, and the dash resets make her extremely hard to kill.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Let the matchup decide how quickly you push. Against early bruisers, farm with Bladesurge and keep the wave close enough that a failed dash chain does not leave you exposed. Against slower tanks, prepare low-health minions, stack Ionian Fervor, and use those resets to take a short trade before dashing back. Defiant Dance reduces the matchup's largest damage spell, but it does not prevent a stun, knockup, or other crowd control. A minion is an escape route only if Bladesurge kills it, so check its health before committing.
gamePlan.midGame: First item gives you real side-lane and river pressure. Crash before moving to Herald, then enter through a wave or a flank where Flawless Duet and Vanguard's Edge can create the first Bladesurge resets. The ultimate's initial barrage marks champions, but crossing its surrounding wall only damages and slows, so do not plan a second dash around the wall. If the enemy sends several champions to answer your side lane, back away through prepared minions and let your team take space elsewhere instead of forcing the outnumbered play.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game, choose between side-lane pressure and a delayed teamfight entry. You can punish a squishy defender in a long lane, but a blind push into several missing enemies wastes the mobility that should make you hard to catch. In grouped fights, let the first control spell land elsewhere, then dash through marked or killable targets to reach a carry. Use Defiant Dance on the largest incoming damage, not as protection from crowd control, and count every available reset before committing.
gamePlan.teamfights: Fight from an angle that gives you a route in and a route out. Vanguard's Edge can mark several champions with its initial barrage, while Flawless Duet either locks the carry or interrupts a diver threatening your own backline. Dash only after identifying the next reset, weave attacks to maintain Ionian Fervor, and hold Defiant Dance for the burst that follows your entry. If the enemy saves reliable crowd control for you, threaten the flank until they spend it rather than giving them an easy target.

primaryRunes.desc: Empower your spell-focused burst with extra damage and scaling for ability-heavy champions.
primaryRunes.note: His ultimate is what upgrades his abilities, so takedowns cutting its cooldown means more upgraded casts per fight.

primaryRunes.note: Ability haste means more turrets and more grenades, which is how much space he controls.

primaryRunes.note: His poke is a rocket volley and back off, and Scorch adds damage to that trade.

secondaryRunes.name: Battle Zeal

secondaryRunes.note: All his damage is basic abilities and the turrets they place, so the amplification builds through a long siege.

spells.name: Flash
spells.note: Must take. Essential for repositioning, escapes, and aggressive combos.

goodAgainst.note: Annie has to walk into turret range to land her combo, and that step up is where the crossfire punishes her, while your grenade stun beats her to the flash all-in.
Brand has no escape and melts to sustained turret damage the moment he commits, and your grenade stun shuts down his combo before he gets a full rotation off.
Twisted Fate is squishy and immobile until his stun card is loaded, so the nest keeps him from ever stepping up to trade, and your shove pins him to his tower instead of roaming.
Ahri can only kill you by diving straight into your crossfire, and a whiffed charm leaves her standing in the turrets with nothing, while your wave clear keeps pace with her roams.

weakAgainst.note: His shadows and dashes skip your crossfire and land him on top of you, where your immobility has no answer to his burst or Death Mark repeating part of the damage he dealt while it was active.
Kassadin blinks past your turrets, and his passive shrugs off your magic poke while he stacks up. After his spike he lands on you faster than you can react, and you have no answer.
Yasuo dashes through your minions and past the turrets, and his wind wall blocks your rockets and grenade outright, so once he reaches you there is no kiting him off.
Irelia dashes off your minions straight onto you, healing through the turret damage with her resets, and your immobility means you cannot peel her off once her stun lands.

gamePlan.overview:
Heimerdinger is the mid laner you pick to own a piece of the map and dare the enemy to walk into it. He drops automated turrets that wear down anyone who lingers, lobs a grenade over terrain and units that slows throughout its explosion but stuns only in the center, and sprays rockets that stop on the first enemy each rocket hits. His strongest damage comes from preparing the turret zone and then landing accurate rockets or the grenade center.

The trade-off is that he is one of the most immobile champions in the game: no dash, no blink, no escape button. Everything good about Heimerdinger happens when he can stand on his nest near a tower or an objective, and everything bad happens when something fast gets past the turrets and onto him.

He is a siege and zone-control specialist, not a duelist. Mid suits him because the short lane lets him set up, deny the enemy farm, and turn the area around Dragon and the mid tower into ground the enemy cannot stand on.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Early on, claim the wave and build your nest somewhere you can defend, usually tucked toward your side so the enemy has to overextend to trade. You push hard with rockets and turrets, so crash waves into tower and zone the enemy off the bounce-back. Hold the grenade for when they step up to last-hit under your turrets, and aim its center for the stun that instantly charges nearby turret beams; an edge hit gives only the slow. Respect any jungler with a gap-closer, since you have no way out of a gank.
gamePlan.midGame: Mid game is where Heimerdinger decides games by setting up on objectives. Place turrets in and around the Dragon pit before the fight starts, and the enemy has to either give up the objective or fight inside your crossfire. In lane, keep shoving so you can drop turrets under their tower and chip it down, since siege is one of your cleanest win conditions. Do not roam far. Instead, ping your team to come to you and the ground you already control rather than chasing fights across the map.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you are either a zoning wall in front of your carries or a siege tool, depending on the map. With your ultimate up you can drop a heavy turret to lock a chokepoint or fire the wide grenade for a long stun on a clumped team. The danger is that one assassin reaching your back line ends your fight instantly, so never walk through fog alone and always keep a peeler or a wall between you and their threats. Position around terrain so divers come at you one at a time, into your turrets instead of onto your body.
gamePlan.teamfights: Heimerdinger wants the fight to come to a spot he already prepared. Lay turrets in the chokepoint your team will defend or contest, then use the upgraded grenade's three large bounces to threaten repeated center stuns as enemies funnel in; touching only an explosion's outer area slows instead. Your job is sustained area damage and lockdown, not chasing, so anchor near your front line and let the enemy eat crossfire trying to reach you. Against heavy dive, save the grenade center as self-peel for whoever jumps you.

boots.name: Spellslinger's Shoes

coreItems.note: Ramping bonus damage and Omnivamp during long fights, which is exactly what her mist forces.

coreItems.name: Rabadon's Deathcap
coreItems.note: Multiplies her ability power, and her passive max health damage scales with it, so this is how she melts a frontline.

coreItems.name: Void Staff
coreItems.note: Cuts magic resist, which is the main answer to Gwen's percent-health magic damage. Choose it over Bloodletter's Curse when Gwen is the team's main magic damage source or enemies have heavy magic resist, since personal penetration matters more than team-wide shred.

coreItems.name: Zhonya's Hourglass
coreItems.note: Build this for when her mist expires and their team is still on top of her. Buy Seeker's Armguard early for the armor and ability power.

situationalItems.name: Morellonomicon
situationalItems.note: Build this when enemies heal through Gwen's sustained damage. Snip Snip and Needlework repeatedly refresh Grievous Wounds during the duel; buy Oblivion Orb early and finish Morellonomicon only when the full stats are worthwhile.

situationalItems.name: Oceanid's Trident
situationalItems.note: Build this when shields absorb Gwen's sustained damage. Repeated Snip Snip and Needlework hits refresh the reduction throughout the duel inside Hallowed Mist.

situationalItems.name: Amaranth's Twinguard
situationalItems.note: Build this when you are fighting in the middle of the enemy team and need both armor and magic resist. Hallowed Mist protects Gwen from outside threats while she activates Twinguard against the enemies fighting inside it.

situationalItems.name: Nashor's Tooth
situationalItems.note: Skip 'n Slash gives Gwen the range and attack speed to land Gnaw repeatedly while stacking Snip Snip. Dusk and Dawn can apply Gnaw a second time on its Spellblade attack, so pair them when the matchup rewards sustained auto-attacking rather than pure spell damage.

situationalItems.name: Malignance
situationalItems.note: Ultimate haste means more of the ranged snips that let her poke from outside melee range.

situationalItems.name: Banshee's Veil
situationalItems.note: Build this when the enemy has crowd control ready for the moment she steps out of her mist.

situationalItems.name: Armored Advance
situationalItems.note: Boot swap against heavy physical damage. Hallowed Mist already denies attacks from outside, and the armor protects Gwen against the melee champions allowed inside it.

situationalItems.name: Chainlaced Crushers
situationalItems.note: Boot swap against heavy magic damage and crowd control, though it gives up the penetration her passive wants.

situationalItems.name: Bloodletter's Curse
situationalItems.note: Build this when Gwen has another magic-damage carry and enemies are stacking magic resist. Her repeated attacks, Snip Snip! hits, and Needlework casts stack Wicked Decay quickly, while the health and ability haste support extended duels. The shred also increases her ally's magic damage.

keystoneRune.name: Conqueror
keystoneRune.desc: Gain stacks by damaging enemy champions. At maximum stacks, gain bonus damage and healing.
keystoneRune.note: Her mist forces long fights, so she reaches max stacks easily and the healing adds to the damage she grinds out.

primaryRunes.name: Demolish
primaryRunes.desc: Charge up a powerful attack against turrets.
primaryRunes.note: She holds a side lane and shoves with her Q, so a won trade turns into tower damage.

primaryRunes.name: Second Wind
primaryRunes.desc: After taking damage from a champion, regenerate health over time.
primaryRunes.note: Her mist covers ranged damage inside it, and this covers the chip she takes stepping out.

primaryRunes.name: Overgrowth
primaryRunes.desc: Gain permanent maximum health when nearby minions or monsters die.
primaryRunes.note: She holds the frontline inside her mist, and the health is what keeps her there through the fight.

secondaryRunes.name: Sudden Impact
secondaryRunes.desc: Deal bonus true damage after using mobility or exiting stealth.
secondaryRunes.note: Her E is a dash, so the bonus true damage lands on the attacks that follow.

spells.name: Flash
spells.note: Must take. Essential for repositioning, escapes, and aggressive combos.

goodAgainst.note: Mundo is one giant health bar and your damage scales off exactly that, so you snip through his regeneration and out-sustain the sustain tank from start to finish.

Realm of Death does steal useful stats, but Gwen can still win inside it because Thousand Cuts and Snip Snip! punish Mordekaiser's health while Skip 'n Slash avoids Obliterate's isolated hit. Do not rely on Hallowed Mist once he is already beside you; hold the dash for his mace swing and stack Snip Snip! before the realm begins.
Sion is an enormous free target: his health pool feeds your passive, his knockup fails against good mist timing, and his shield melts under true damage.
All that armor and no magic resist: your snips are percent-health magic damage and your Q center is true damage, so his armor stacking does nothing. His wide-radius ultimate is his only real threat.

weakAgainst.note: Apprehend can drag Gwen out of Hallowed Mist, while Hemorrhage makes early extended trades dangerous. Noxian Guillotine is stack-scaled true damage rather than a fixed execute, so track bleed stacks and use the mist's defenses to deny his setup before items let Gwen win the sustained duel.

Spinning Slash keeps Tryndamere in melee where Hallowed Mist offers no protection, and Undying Rage lets him continue attacking after Gwen's final Snip Snip! would normally finish the duel. Slow him with Needlework, save Skip 'n Slash to kite the undying window, and re-enter only after the ultimate expires.

Shen's block stops your flurries when it matters, and his taunt pulls you out of the mist into a trade on his terms. His sustain means your snips never quite finish him, so he freely pressures the map with ult roams.
Wukong reaches you whether the mist is up or not: he waits out the cloud, bursts you before your sustain matters, and the clone baits the mist you were saving for his real combo.

gamePlan.overview:
Gwen is built to punish health-stacking frontliners. Her scissors deal percentage maximum-health magic damage and heal her as they cut, while the center of Snip Snip! deals true damage. A large health pool gives Thousand Cuts more value, but Gwen still needs time and spacing to reach four Q stacks and complete her rotation.

Hallowed Mist is her signature trick: a drifting cloud that makes her untargetable to anyone outside it. Enemies either step into the mist and fight on her terms or wait it out while she snips freely. Whole trades, ganks, and tower dives fail inside that cloud, which makes her one of the safest scaling picks in the lane.

She struggles against opponents who refuse to enter the cloud: ranged poke that chips her between mists, and hard duelists who beat her at melee. Gwen wins by reaching her items and forcing every fight to happen inside her mist.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Trade where the mist favors you. Build Snippy stacks with attacks, use Snip Snip's center for true damage, and drop Hallowed Mist when a ranged opponent answers. Gwen is untargetable only to enemies outside the mist; an enemy who steps inside can target her normally, though she still gains armor and magic resistance. Against ranged poke, farm patiently and save the cloud for their commit.
gamePlan.midGame: After the first item, push the Baron wave when you know where the enemy jungler is and pressure the turret only while Hallowed Mist can cover the retreat. Crash before moving toward Herald, then use Needlework to slow enemies entering the river fight. Its Wild Rift recasts unlock after their static cooldowns and do not require an attack or ability hit, so begin the sequence early enough to reach the three- and five-needle volleys. If several enemies answer the side lane, retreat through your vision and let the team take space elsewhere.
gamePlan.lateGame: Push the side wave only when you can join Baron or Elder before the enemy starts it. In grouped fights, place Hallowed Mist so Gwen can damage the frontline while remaining outside the enemy backline's targeting range. Move toward a carry only after the control that can stop Skip 'n Slash is used. If the mist expires or shifts away from the fight, step back and wait for another safe damage window rather than continuing in open ground.
gamePlan.teamfights: Fight from inside the mist or not at all. Open on their frontline, snipping the biggest health bars while the mist blocks their focus, and let your ultimate's needles slow and chunk the group. When their tanks melt, and they will, the mist walks you to the backline next. The discipline is cloud timing: drop it as their damage commits, not before, and reposition with E so the fight stays inside your mist.

situationalItems.note: Build this when the enemy has crowd control ready for his E, which is the one thing that stops an engage he has committed to.

Choose it when enemies have not built much magic resist, so trading Void Staff's extra damage for more ability haste and an area heal after takedowns is worthwhile.

keystoneRune.note: His E, cask and empowered attack are three quick hits, and the move speed is how he leaves a fight he just opened.

primaryRunes.desc: Deal bonus true damage after using mobility or exiting stealth.
primaryRunes.note: His E is a dash, so the bonus true damage triggers as Body Slam connects.

primaryRunes.name: Chain Assault

primaryRunes.note: His combo lands on whoever he barrels into, and this rewards committing all of it to that target.

primaryRunes.name: Eyeball Collector
primaryRunes.desc: Gain adaptive force by collecting takedown stacks from enemy champions and epic monsters.
primaryRunes.note: His ganks convert into kills through the knockback setup, and each takedown adds damage to the next one.

secondaryRunes.name: Transcendence
secondaryRunes.desc: Gain ability haste, then reduce a basic ability's cooldown after it hits at level 9.
secondaryRunes.note: Ability haste means more casks and more dashes, which is his clear speed and his gank frequency.

spells.name: Flash
spells.note: Must take. Essential for repositioning, escapes, and aggressive combos.

spells.name: Smite
spells.note: Required for Jungling. Secures objectives and sustains through camp clears.

goodAgainst.note: Master Yi cannot do much to you until he has items, and your cask, slam, and ult form a full lockdown chain that interrupts his Alpha Strike and flings him out of the fight.
Kindred relies on kiting, but Body Slam closes the gap her kiting needs, and your burst combo deletes her fragile frame once you land it. Drunken Rage also shrugs off her poke.
Warwick needs the long drain fight, and you refuse to give it: your cask chunks him before he engages, Drunken Rage shrugs off the damage his sustain relies on, and your burst out-trades him.

weakAgainst.note: Zed swaps away from your telegraphed Barrel Roll and Body Slam with his shadow, then pokes you with shuriken from a range your combo cannot answer. He refuses the trade you win and takes the one you do not.
Nunu out-sizes you: his percent-health bite chunks your health faster than your combo dents his, he sustains through your poke, and his snowball catches you the moment Body Slam is down.
Diana's shield absorbs your Body Slam burst and her pull stops you from kiting away with Explosive Cask. She dives, resets her combo, and out-damages a brawler whose burst she just soaked up.

gamePlan.overview:
Gragas is a tanky AP brawler built around his cask and Body Slam. He clears fast, pokes and zones from long range with the cask, uses Body Slam as both gap closer and escape, and his ultimate knocks a target wherever he wants it. That last button is the reason to pick him: he gets to decide where the enemy carry stands.

His ganks land harder than they look. Body Slam closes the distance and the cask slow gives your laner a free window, so a gank into a pushed lane once his clear is done usually means a flash burned or a kill outright. He is not a snowballing assassin, though. Gragas wants to farm to his first item, build resists, and arrive at the dragon pit as the bruiser nobody wants to fight in a tight space.

The catch is that he leans on cooldowns. Once the cask and slam are spent, he has no follow-up for a few seconds, and fast early junglers love catching him in that gap. His single-target damage also thins out late, but played for tempo and the fight-flipping ultimate, he is one of the safest playmakers in the role.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Gragas can choose between a stable full clear and an early Body Slam gank. After three camps, check for a lane where the target has crossed the midpoint or allied control can guarantee the slam. Lead with Barrel Roll to slow the escape, hold Body Slam until the target commits to a direction, and use Happy Hour to leave the play healthy. If the angle is weak, keep farming toward Explosive Cask rather than showing on the map for nothing.

At scuttle, fight around your cooldowns instead of trading basic attacks with a dedicated duelist. Body Slam can interrupt an approach or secure space for Smite, but missing it leaves you exposed. Track the enemy start, keep a ward on the entrance they are likely to use, and make your first move toward the lane that can actually convert the displacement.
gamePlan.midGame:
Tight river spaces amplify every part of the Gragas displacement kit. Set vision early and look to flip a dragon or Herald fight with one good ultimate that knocks their tank off the pit or their carry into your front line. That swing is worth contesting whenever your team is winning the early skirmishes. In an even game take Herald, since it becomes a tower without asking your team to hold the fight, and save the dragon priority for a comp that genuinely wants soul.

This is also your window to invade the weaker clearers, because you out-sustain and out-bully many junglers once your resists come in. Steal their camps, push them off scuttle, and keep clearing between plays so you never fall behind on levels.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game your job changes from killing enemies to moving them. The burst that deleted squishies earlier now only chunks them, so stop hunting solo kills and start hunting positioning. You are the one who walks up, takes the first wave of crowd control on stacked resists, and throws their carry over the wall into your waiting team. Body Slam becomes as much an escape as an engage now, so save it for when you are out of position instead of spending it on poke. Around Baron you are the best disengage on your team: a cask onto a stacked enemy, or an ult that flings their initiator off the pit, can turn a lost objective into a clean reset. That disruption is worth more than any damage you would have added.
gamePlan.teamfights: You start the fight or you ruin theirs, and most games it is the former. The clean opener is a flash-ult or a deep Body Slam that drops their carry inside your team, then you sit on top of them while everyone collapses, soaking damage on your resists. If their engage comes first, flip it: knock their initiating tank or assassin straight back out of the fight with your ult and the whole thing falls apart before it starts. Cask the chokepoint to split their group or zone the backline off the objective, and keep Body Slam in your pocket as an escape once the ult is spent. The mistake that loses Gragas fights is a greedy ult that knocks an enemy toward safety, so pick the target and the direction before you press the button.

boots.name: Crimson Lucidity

coreItems.name: Redemption

coreItems.note: Build this when Janna must influence fights beyond her immediate shield range. Redemption can land as Monsoon disengages the enemy, layering another area heal onto the allies she just separated from danger.

coreItems.name: Banshee's Veil
coreItems.note: Build this when the enemy has a hook or point-and-click stun, since she is the most fragile champion on the map.

situationalItems.name: Mikael's Blessing
situationalItems.note: Build this when a carry is losing fights to one removable stun or root. Mikael's cleanses the lockdown, then Eye of the Storm and Monsoon cover the burst that follows.

situationalItems.name: Shurelya's Battlesong
situationalItems.note: Team-wide speed on top of her passive, which turns a disengage into everyone repositioning at once.

keystoneRune.name: Aery
keystoneRune.desc: Your attacks and abilities send Aery to a target, dealing damage to enemies or shielding allies.
keystoneRune.note: Aery follows her shield as well as her damage, so it pays out on the button she presses most.

primaryRunes.desc: Damaging enemy champions heals you and the lowest-health nearby ally after a short cooldown.
primaryRunes.note: Her Q can hit an enemy champion to heal her and the lowest-Health allied champion nearby when the rune is ready.
