Mel out-ranges you and her reflect punishes anyone who commits a big combo into it, but she has no dash and her snare is her only peel, so she cannot escape once you close.

weakAgainst.note: Zed is the classic squishy-mage killer, and you are the target he wants: no burst defense and one dash. His shadow baits out Lightning Rush, and his ultimate marks a kill you cannot survive.

His pole vault and trickster dodge sidestep your shuriken and your ultimate, so landing marks on him is frustrating. He all-ins through your poke and you have nothing to disengage with once he commits.

His targeted root catches you out of Lightning Rush into a combo your thin frame cannot survive. His health, itemization and movement-speed proc also help him manage your shuriken poke, and he out-scales the lane.
Her charm and three dashes let her dodge your marks, pick every trade, and delete your squishy frame. You cannot reliably stack the storm on a target that slips each commit.

His periodic magic-damage shield absorbs your shuriken and storm, and he is too tanky to kill easily. His taunt and knockup punish your committed dive, while his long-range but limited Hero's Entrance can counter a roam by targeting an allied champion within range.

gamePlan.overview:
Kennen plays like a ranged caster in lane but fights like a melee bruiser in teamfights. He runs on energy instead of mana, but repeated casts can still empty the bar. Thundering Shuriken stops on the first enemy hit, so using it on the wave does not also poke a champion behind the minions. The kit is built around stacking Marks of the Storm: land three on someone and they are stunned and Kennen restores energy, which makes careful ability sequencing central to his pressure.

In lane he is all about tempo. You hard-shove with shuriken, deny the enemy farm with chip damage, then use that timer to roam or set up your jungler. He has little upfront burst before items and no second escape, so early game means pushing hard without getting collapsed on.

He is strongest in mid- and late-game flanks. Slicing Maelstrom can stun several grouped enemies, and a Flash angle from fog can reach the backline before it spreads out. Kennen is squishy and committal, so enter only when his team can follow or the key defensive cooldowns have been spent.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Play the lane around the shuriken. Spam it for poke and to keep the wave pushing toward the enemy tower, which starves them of farm and frees you to roam. Be careful with Lightning Rush: it is your only mobility and your only real way to dodge a gank, so burning it for an aggressive mark leaves you stranded if their jungler shows. Respect dive comps and roaming junglers, because a squishy Kennen with his dash down is free for anyone who collapses on him.
gamePlan.midGame: This is where your lane tempo pays off. Once you have a couple of items and your ultimate, group and roam with the wave shoved. You are best at catching grouped enemies around objectives, so hover the edges of fights and wait for the enemy to clump for a dragon or a tower push. Side-laning is fine for the waveclear, but your real value is being ready to flank, so do not wander so far that you cannot reach the fight when it starts.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game Kennen is a flanker and a teamfight finisher, not a duelist. With full items your Maelstrom flank can chain-stun and burst a clustered backline, but if you get caught alone you die without giving your team anything. Vision and patience matter: scout the angle, find the flank, and commit only when the storm will land on several high-value targets. One well-timed engage from the fog can decide the fight; a mistimed one throws the game.
gamePlan.teamfights: Kennen is a flank champion, so your job is finding an angle the enemy is not watching. The best case is a Flash into the middle of their grouped team, dropping Slicing Maelstrom so its three marks stun each enemy it keeps hitting. The ultimate alone can stun a target once; combine Electrical Surge, Lightning Rush, a shuriken, or the empowered attack to start or finish another mark cycle. The catch is total commitment: you have no second escape, so only go in when the payoff is multiple stunned enemies, otherwise you are just feeding a pick.

gamePlan.overview:
Kennen is a counterpick most melee Baron laners hate. A ranged yordle in a lane full of melee fighters, he punishes every last hit with shurikens and electrified attacks, and every third mark of the storm stuns the target. Lane bullies arrive expecting to bully and instead pay health for every minion they take.

What sets him apart from other ranged Baron laners is the teamfight. Slicing Maelstrom can place three marks and stun each enemy caught inside it, so a flank angle threatens several targets at once. He uses energy instead of mana, but repeated casts can still empty the bar if he misses the refund from completing three marks.

His weaknesses are obvious. He is tiny, squishy, and one clean gap close away from dying. Kennen games come down to spacing: he wins it at range all laning phase, then bets the late game on landing one perfect storm.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Hold the wave where you can pressure last-hits without exposing yourself to a long chase. Use Thundering Shuriken when the opponent steps away from the minion line, then threaten the third mark with Electrical Surge or the empowered attack. Keep enough energy and Lightning Rush available when the enemy gap closer or jungler can reach you. If repeated poke is pushing the wave, ward before following it toward the enemy turret and let the wave return rather than trading inside a gank angle.
gamePlan.midGame: Crash the Baron wave before moving to Herald or dragon, then approach through a route the enemy has not already warded. Look for a Lightning Rush or Flash angle that places Slicing Maelstrom on two or more important targets, but wait for the crowd control that can stop your entry to be used first. If no flank exists, poke beside your frontline and hold the ultimate to counter the enemy engage. Avoid extending a side lane when the next objective is close, because your grouped impact is worth more than one extra wave.
gamePlan.lateGame: Push a side wave only when you can rejoin before Baron or Elder becomes contestable. In the setup, use vision denial to hold a side angle and keep Lightning Rush available until the enemy formation is visible. Enter when Slicing Maelstrom can reach the backline without crossing every enemy control spell. If that route never opens, stay with your carry and use the marks to stun divers instead of forcing an entry.
gamePlan.teamfights: Poke from range while tracking the spells that can interrupt or burst you on entry. When the enemy backline groups and those cooldowns are unavailable, use Lightning Rush or Flash to place Slicing Maelstrom across the cluster. Electrical Surge, Thundering Shuriken, and the empowered attack can complete another mark cycle after the ultimate's stun. If divers reach your carry first, stay back and complete the stun on them rather than abandoning your team for a flank.

gamePlan.overview:
Kha'Zix is an evolving assassin who is strongest against isolated targets. Taste Their Fear deals much more damage when no allied unit is close to the victim, Void Spike provides ranged pressure and healing, and Leap closes the gap. Evolutions can extend his jump, widen and improve his spikes, or strengthen the stealth pattern, so the best choice depends on how he can reach and leave each fight.

He wins with early tempo and snowballing picks. His clear is fast, so he reaches his gank levels quickly and starts hunting the moment a lane overextends. You are not farming toward a teamfight ultimate or frontlining anything. You are leaping onto an isolated jungler at scuttle, deleting a mid laner who walked too far, and using the reset leap to reach a second body before the first one dies.

The catch is that Kha'Zix gets much less value when enemies stay grouped. Hard crowd control can stop his leap, a tank frontline can block access to a carry, and his thin health bar gives him little time to recover from a poor entry. He needs to use early tempo before teams group tightly around objectives.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Your first clear is genuinely quick: the isolation bonus shreds buffs and big monsters, so you finish the full rotation with a tempo lead. Take scuttle on the way through, which puts you on level five, and then that tempo is what opens the hunt. While your camps respawn, find the lane that pushed too far, leap the wall onto the isolated target, and burst them before help arrives. Evolving Taste Their Fear first does not add raw damage; it adds attack and Q range and refunds 40% of Q's cooldown against isolated targets, improving repeated damage once a gank or objective fight lasts beyond the opening hit. Clear again when the camps are back and repeat.

Contest Scuttle when the duel and nearby lane priority favor you. Against a stronger early fighter, give up the direct river contest and use tracking information to take the opposite crab or an exposed camp. An invade is valuable only when you can leave before the enemy lanes collapse, so keep Leap available and do not trade your life for one buff.
gamePlan.midGame:
Approach early objectives as opportunities to isolate a rotation, not as front-to-back brawls. Catch someone walking to dragon or Herald alone and the fight becomes a free five on four, which is worth doing whenever your team is ahead. In an even game take Herald and trade dragon away, since a tower suits your tempo better than a soul your comp may never cash in, though a team built to fight is a reason to flip that.

Between objectives keep the loop tight: clear a camp, leap into a lane, kill the isolated carry, and use the takedown reset to leave; but only after evolving Leap. Hunt the enemy jungler on his own side and steal his camps while he clears, because letting the mid game stall hands the scalers the time they need to outgrow your single-target ceiling.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you are a backline removal tool, not a fight starter, so your fights begin from the fog with an enemy carry already isolated in your sights. Wait for them to drift a step from their peel, use Void Assault to trigger Unseen Threat and approach, then burst them and spend a remaining recast or an Evolved Wings reset to escape before lockdown lands. Takedowns do not reset Void Assault. The enemy comp works against you now: a tank wall and a clustered team mean the isolation bonus rarely triggers, and one clean crowd-control chain ends you. Around Baron and the late dragons, look for the flank pick that thins their numbers before the real fight, since removing a carry before the engage does more than jumping into the middle of everyone. If they group and hold vision, your contribution is patience: find the one isolated mistake and punish it completely.
gamePlan.teamfights: You are not in the opening clash, you are circling it. Let the engage happen, let their backline focus your frontline, then leap onto the carry the moment they stand a step too far from their support. The isolation bonus is the whole point, so the angle matters more than the timing: hunt the target with the fewest allies close by, not the closest one. Land the kill and your leap refreshes, letting you move to the next priority target instead of getting caught by their peel. Evolved stealth is your escape when a fight goes wrong, so vanish, reset your cooldowns, and re-enter rather than feeding your fragile body into their crowd control. If their formation holds tight and nobody isolates, do not force the dive; threaten the flank, make their carry flinch and reposition, and take the pick the instant their discipline slips.

gamePlan.overview:
Lee Sin is an early-tempo jungler with several ways to enter or reshape a skirmish. Sonic Wave marks a target for Resonating Strike, Safeguard crosses terrain and shields him, and Flurry rewards attacks between ability casts. Dragon's Rage can remove a diver, displace a carry toward Lee Sin's team, or knock one enemy through others. His impact depends on using that mobility before farming junglers reach their later spikes.

He wins with tempo. His clear is fast and his levels come quick, so he hits his gank threshold ahead of slower junglers and turns it into a lead before anyone has items. He wins the scuttle fight, the invade, and most early one-on-ones, because his shield and the healing off Iron Will out-brawl the farm-focused junglers while they are still building toward their spike. Played well, he is less a farming jungler than a tempo threat the enemy is racing against.

His weakness is built into that identity: Lee Sin is front-loaded and on a timer. He scales worse than almost everyone he beats early. If you do not convert the lead into towers, objectives, and dead carries, the tanks get unkillable, the carries out-range your dashes, and the monk who ran the map is left with one kick and little else. Snowball or fade.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Lee Sin does not need to wait for Dragon's Rage before affecting a lane. Clear three or four camps, then read the map: Sonic Wave and Safeguard can punish an overextended lane, protect an ally from a dive, or invade a weaker jungler when your nearby lanes can move. If none of those plays is clearly available, finish the full clear and take the safe level-five timing instead of manufacturing action.

At scuttle, preserve Safeguard as a way to follow an ally or leave after Resonating Strike commits you. Once Dragon's Rage is unlocked, approach from the side and kick the target toward your laner rather than using the ultimate only as extra damage. Lee Sin's early game is about converting real openings before other junglers scale, not abandoning camps for a hopeful gank.
gamePlan.midGame:
Dragon Rage makes the first contested pit a displacement puzzle Lee Sin is built to solve. Herald is your kind of objective, since your gank pressure can clear the nearby lanes before you start it. Around dragon, kick their jungler away from the pit or boot a carry into your team before the Smite war begins. Contest both when your team is winning early fights, and prioritise the dragon when its permanent team buff or the nearby fight is worth more than Herald's tower pressure.

Between objectives, keep the loop going but spend it aggressively. Every minute spent power-farming brings your fading curve closer, so trade tempo for kills while you are still the strongest champion on the field.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game asks a different question, and raw stats are no longer the answer. You will not out-duel a full-build bruiser or out-trade a fed carry in a straight fight, so look for the one kick that matters. Hop into a flank and kick their most important player toward your team, or kick a frontline champion through clustered enemies so the collision damages and knocks them up. Hitting terrain has no special bonus. At Baron and Elder, displace the enemy jungler from Smite range or combine missing-health Resonating Strike with Smite for your own secure.
gamePlan.teamfights: Your job in a fight is to reach one person, usually their carry or highest-value target. The classic play is the flank: Safeguard over a wall from an angle they are not watching, kick the priority target back into your team where every cooldown lands on them at once, and chase the cleanup with the rest of your kit. If the kick is not there, peeling is just as valuable: Safeguard back to your carry to body-block a diver, cripple their frontline to slow the engage, and use your mobility to never be the one who gets caught. The mistake to avoid is the lonely flash-kick into five people, because trading yourself for nothing gives away the one tool that makes you scary. Pick the moment and land the kick; a carry displaced into your team usually decides the rest.

Ring of Frost is an area cast rather than a projectile, but Fizz is untargetable during Playful and can avoid the root until he lands. Hold W or the targeted ultimate for his landing instead of casting into the untargetable window.

weakAgainst.note: Bouncing Bomb and Hexplosive Minefield clear from beyond Lissandra's short spell range, while Satchel Charge escapes the visible path of Glacial Path. Vel'Koz's artillery out-ranges Lissandra's direct trading tools, and his channeled ultimate punishes a predictable walk into Ring of Frost range. Use Glacial Path from fog or save Frozen Tomb to stop the channel once you reach him.
Her sphere poke out-ranges your whole kit, and her stun sets up a burst your short-range kit cannot answer in a straight trade.

Riftwalk lets Kassadin avoid the area before Ring of Frost lands or punish Glacial Path's visible destination, but it cannot undo a root or the targeted Frozen Tomb stun that has already connected. Pressure his early wave and hold the instant control for after he blinks in.

gamePlan.overview:
Lissandra is a control mage built to punish committed assassins. Ice Shard slows and shatters on the first enemy hit, becoming wider and traveling farther behind that target, so minions can extend her poke. Ring of Frost roots nearby enemies. Glacial Path damages along a visible traveling claw and lets Lissandra blink to its current location on recast. Frozen Tomb either knocks down and stuns an enemy champion for 1.5 seconds or places Lissandra in 2.5 seconds of self-stasis while healing her, with both versions creating a damaging slow field.

In Wild Rift she wins by holding the lane steady, then turning mid-game skirmishes into locked-down picks. Nearby enemy champion deaths also spawn Frozen Thralls that chase visible enemies, slow around themselves, and explode after four seconds, so the first takedown can spread damage through a clustered fight. Because Frozen Tomb has two mutually exclusive casts, each engage must choose between stunning one enemy and using the self-cast heal and stasis.

Her main weakness is reliable reach. Longer-range mages can chip her down while Glacial Path's slow-moving claw telegraphs the blink destination. E is a real escape and can cross terrain, but it needs time to travel and Lissandra must recast before the claw disappears, so immediate pressure can still trap her.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Lane patiently and trade through the wave. Aim Ice Shard into a minion so the shattered extension reaches a champion behind it, then use Ring of Frost when a melee opponent actually enters its radius. Glacial Path is both engage and escape: send it toward safety before danger reaches you, because the claw takes time to travel and the recast is unavailable for its first half-second. Against assassins, hold the instant area root for after their gap-close.
gamePlan.midGame: Once your first item and ultimate are available, shove the wave before moving with your jungler. A roam that catches an overextended carry with Ring of Frost can be worth more than the next minion, but a failed rotation should not cost several waves. At six minutes, use mid priority to reach the safer of Herald or dragon first. Herald is usually the stronger even conversion, while dragon is the better plan when your composition can keep winning grouped fights toward soul. Glacial Path creates the flank and Frozen Tomb removes the champion who could contest, so approach from controlled vision rather than showing the engage from mid lane.
gamePlan.lateGame: You are the lockdown your team plays around, not the carry they protect. Your value is landing the enemy-cast tomb on the right target or choosing self-stasis when a deep area root matters more. Push a side lane only with a safe Glacial Path route prepared; without Frozen Tomb you still have an escape blink, but no instant invulnerability or targeted stun. In grouped fights, a first takedown also creates a Frozen Thrall that can chase and explode through the enemy formation.
gamePlan.teamfights: Choose the Frozen Tomb mode before committing. For a pick, Flash or Glacial Path into Ring of Frost and cast Frozen Tomb on the priority enemy for the 1.5-second stun. For a deep area engage, blink into several enemies, root them with W, then self-cast Frozen Tomb for healing and 2.5 seconds of stasis while its field slows and damages around you. You cannot stun an enemy with R and then self-cast the same ultimate. If the first target dies nearby, position the resulting Frozen Thrall so its chase and explosion pressure the rest of the team.

weakAgainst.note: Black Shield can deny Twisted Advance's root and leave you committed beside its target. Morgana cannot hit untargetable Maokai during the dash, but she can aim Dark Binding at the arrival point, so wait out the shield before committing.
His cleanse pops your root off the target the moment it lands, which deletes the whole point of your dash, and his speed-ups pull his carry out of your kill window.
Lux pokes and bursts from outside your dash range, and her binding catches you the moment you try to close, turning your engage attempt into a death sentence.

Galio's magic shield and bulk absorb sapling damage, but they do not prevent Twisted Advance's root. The real problem is the return engage: once Maokai arrives, Galio can taunt him and protect the nearby carry.

Braum can dash to the rooted carry and grant both of them resistances, then build Concussive Blows on Maokai during the melee trade. Unbreakable does not erase a planted sapling's area explosion, and Braum has no basic-ability flip, but Glacial Fissure and Bramble Smash can counter-engage each other.

gamePlan.overview:
Maokai fills the Dragon lane with saplings the enemy has to play around. Sap Magic periodically empowers his next basic attack to heal him; Maokai's own casts, enemy abilities that hit him, and Sapling Toss hits on champions or epic monsters reduce that passive cooldown. Twisted Advance makes him untargetable during its targeted dash and roots on arrival, while Nature's Grasp sends five brambles forward that each stop on the first champion hit.

In the 2v2 he is a durable walking root. A normal sapling grants sight for 20 seconds, chases nearby enemies, then explodes and slows. A sapling placed in brush lasts 30 seconds and deals double damage across three bursts, making brush placement a major part of Maokai's lane pressure rather than only a vision trick.

The catch is range and timing. Twisted Advance is a short targeted dash, so a cleanse or immediate disengage can leave Maokai committed between the enemy duo. He needs allies close enough to follow the root, and he must keep enough health to survive until Bramble Smash is available for the next peel or knockback.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Prioritize brush saplings when an enemy is likely to trigger them, because their double damage arrives as three bursts; a lane sapling deals less but can pressure the wave. Hold Twisted Advance until the root buys real follow-up. Sap Magic heals on its empowered basic attack only when Maokai is below 95% health, and casting abilities or being hit by enemy abilities reduces that passive cooldown, so weave the attack once it is ready rather than expecting automatic healing from nearby spell casts.
gamePlan.midGame: Before dragon or Herald, move with a teammate to place vision and seed likely entrances with Sapling Toss. Cast Nature's Grasp through a choke when your team can follow the roots, then use Twisted Advance on the highest-value reachable target. Roam after the Dragon-lane wave is safe rather than assuming Maokai's durability will rescue a failed trip. In grouped skirmishes, decide whether the first root starts the engage or stops a diver from reaching your carry.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you are the lockdown that opens every fight and the body that refuses to die in it. The creeping ultimate starts fights and zones at the same time: rolled through a choke it splits their team, and saved for the engage it snares whoever leads. Around Baron and dragon, set the trap, root the first target your team can collapse on, then fall back to peel for your carry once the burst goes out. You bring almost no damage, so your value is the snare and the frontline, which means staying alive matters more than any chase. An alive Maokai keeps applying crowd control; a dead one gave one engage and nothing more.
gamePlan.teamfights: Start the fight or split it. The best opening is the vine wall rolling into a clustered team and rooting two or more while your side collapses, but the wall is just as useful rolled sideways to cut their backline off from the fight. After the engage, switch jobs: Twisted Advance becomes peel for the diver on your carry, and your body stands between your ADC and everything that wants them. Keep saplings in the chokes so flanks show up before they arrive. You will not top the damage chart and should not try; the fight you win is the one where the snare hit the right target and your carry survived.

goodAgainst.note: Seraphine is immobile, but Beat Drop can root or stun under the right conditions and Encore charms through multiple targets, so she has more than one way to disrupt the dive. Engage after either control spell misses and keep Eclipse active through her return damage.

Lulu can polymorph Leona after Zenith Blade and Wild Growth can knock up nearby enemies while giving the target health and a slowing aura. Bait one of those major peel tools or lock Lulu herself before committing the full chain.

Sona is fragile and has no basic hard crowd control, but Crescendo is a real area stun and Song of Celerity helps her duo create space. Track the ultimate, then punish her low durability when it is unavailable.

Detached Yuumi is vulnerable, but an attached Yuumi is untargetable while her host remains fully mobile, not stationary. Lock down the host before Yuumi's healing, shielding, and Final Chapter's stacking slow can turn the extended fight.
The engage mirror goes your way up close: your resists and Sunlight burst out-brawl his slower chain, and his hook needs a clear path while your Zenith Blade threatens whenever he plants his feet.

His shield blocks your engage and his passive stun wins the brawl after it, so he soaks your whole chain on his own body and his team punishes a Leona with no cooldowns left.
The lantern pulls your pinned target out of the kill before your ADC finishes, and his hook plus flay out-trade your walk-in while he is tanky enough to survive your chain.

Black Shield can deny your initial control chain, since every stun, snare and Solar Flare is crowd control. Bait it, swap targets, or coordinate magic damage to break it before committing the rest of your lockdown.

gamePlan.overview:
Leona is a direct hard-engage support built around reaching one enemy and holding them for her team. Shield of Daybreak resets her attack and empowers the next hit to stun. Eclipse grants bonus armor and magic resistance; not flat damage reduction; and keeps those defenses for another three seconds if its delayed explosion hits an enemy. Zenith Blade damages everything in its line but roots and dashes Leona to the furthest champion hit. Solar Flare then stuns only its center while the outer area applies a heavy slow.

In the Dragon lane she is the engage. Each damaging ability applies Sunlight for 1.5 seconds, and only another allied champion's damage consumes it for bonus magic damage, so space the control chain so your carry can trigger each mark. She pairs best with carries who punish a stunned target instantly, and her warding is roam-focused: watch the river and turn her engage range into picks across the map.

Her flaw is her strength: once she commits, she is all in. No escape, no disengage, no poke to fall back on. If her target gets peeled away or cleansed, she is a melee tank stuck in the enemy backline with every cooldown spent.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Play the early lane as a constant engage threat, not a poke support. Zenith Blade is ranged but commits Leona to the furthest champion it hits, so wait for the enemy carry to step into a line that does not drag you onto the wrong target. Activate Eclipse before arriving, then use Shield of Daybreak's attack reset and leave brief windows for your carry to consume repeated Sunlight marks. Ward the bushes and river entrance early: a Leona who knows where the jungler is can commit safely, while a blind one may dash into a countergank.
gamePlan.midGame: Mid game your engage threat covers the map. Solar Flare starts fights from outside their vision, so roam mid or pinch the river before objectives and look for a stun onto anyone out of position. Around dragon and herald you decide when the fight starts: engage the enemy carry or their support and let your team collapse on the pinned target. Keep warding the pit approaches so your dive lands on your terms, and remember that turning lane priority into a pick is worth more than another minion.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game, choose between starting the fight and holding your control for counter-engage. If your team can follow, use vision denial to approach a reachable carry and activate Eclipse before committing. Against several divers, stay near your own carry and chain Shield of Daybreak into Solar Flare after the first enemy enters. An unsupported engage leaves Leona stranded, so check ally distance before using Zenith Blade.
gamePlan.teamfights: Your fight is one decision made well: who to stun and when. Start with Solar Flare from range or Zenith Blade through the frontline, then place Shield of Daybreak's reliable stun where it prevents an escape. Eclipse's resistances, extended by hitting an enemy with the explosion, help survive the focus that follows. Peeling is also on the table: the attack stun and Solar Flare center can lock a diver off your carry, while the outer flare only slows. Space abilities so allies can consume each Sunlight mark rather than overlapping every cast instantly.

goodAgainst.note: Both of you are immobile, but you out-range him before his stacks come online, so he takes poke on every last hit. The lane only turns if his cage and stacks get enough time.
Annie's reach is far shorter than yours, so she has to walk through your poke to do anything, and her only threat is a loaded stun she cannot force onto you at range.

Light Binding and Lucent Singularity reach beyond Sear and Pillar of Flame, while Prismatic Barrier can blunt the Blaze detonation after Brand uses targeted Conflagration. Pressure from maximum range, stand away from the minion he can spread fire through, and commit Final Spark after Sear misses so his stun cannot interrupt the setup.
Ryze wants to scale, and your range lets you poke him off every last hit before he gets there. His combos out-damage you once he has items, so the lane is only easy while he is behind.

Rebuttal can destroy and reflect Light Binding because Q is a hostile projectile, but Final Spark is a laser rather than a projectile and cannot be reflected. Bait the 0.75-second invulnerability before firing the rest of the combo.

weakAgainst.note: Wind Wall blocks Light Binding and the travelling Lucent Singularity, but it cannot block Final Spark because the laser is not a projectile. Respect his wave dashes while those first two spells are unavailable.
Your root is a slow skillshot he sidesteps with his shadow, and the moment it is on cooldown he has a free window to kill you.

Akali's shroud prevents basic-attack targeting, but Lux's Q, E, and global laser are aimed casts that can still hit its area. The danger is Akali's dashes avoiding Binding and reaching an immobile Lux, so hold E's automatic slow around the likely exit.

Playful/Trickster makes Fizz untargetable through Light Binding and can also avoid Final Spark, while Chum the Waters forces Lux to spend her only peel under his all-in. Hold Binding until he lands from the hop, keep the wave near your turret after level five, and punish with a full rotation only while Playful/Trickster is on cooldown.

Katarina can Shunpo between daggers to avoid Binding. If Q hits during Death Lotus it roots her movement but does not interrupt the channel, so Lux must burst her, use stasis, or rely on an ally's interrupt rather than treating root as a cancel.

gamePlan.overview:
Lux is an artillery mage with unusually strong lane control and global map reach. Light Binding travels through minions, damages them, and only stops early after rooting up to two champions or large monsters, so standing inside the wave does not protect the enemy mid laner. Lucent Singularity grants sight and remains on empty ground, but Lux cannot recast it: it automatically detonates as soon as an enemy enters its area. Final Spark is a global directional laser, not merely a long-range finisher, so Lux can influence distant fights and objectives without leaving mid.

In mid she plays around wave control, poke, and picks. Lucent Singularity clears grouped minions while Light Binding can damage the wave and threaten a root through it. After crashing, Lux can move toward river, protect an ally with Prismatic Barrier, or threaten a binding from fog. Final Spark adds long-range follow-up, but the root still needs allied damage or a safe full rotation to become a kill.

The catch is that she has no dash, blink, or self-speed. Missing Light Binding removes her hard control, but she still has Lucent Singularity's automatic slow and Prismatic Barrier's two-pass shield; use those to retreat rather than treating the rest of the kit as empty.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Use Lucent Singularity across grouped minions, then line Light Binding through the wave to finish the clear. Q passes through minions and deals 90% damage to them, so a good angle can push the wave and root the enemy mid laner standing behind it at the same time. E automatically explodes when any enemy enters its area; you cannot hold it beneath a target or choose a later detonation. To use it for vision or zoning, place it on empty ground along the route the enemy would need to cross. You have no escape, so ward the river and keep Q available when an assassin can punish the shove.
gamePlan.midGame: This is where Lux becomes a map threat. Clear quickly with E-Q, then either move on the priority you created or stay safe in mid and aim Final Spark at a side-lane fight. Its range is global, so check the other lanes whenever opponents are rooted, recalling on low health, or fighting in a predictable path. Around dragon, herald, and baron, Lucent Singularity gives sight until an enemy enters and triggers it, while the global laser can finish or steal an objective if you track its health carefully. Keep sight of the enemy assassin, since getting caught while watching another lane is the mistake an immobile champion cannot afford.
gamePlan.lateGame: By now one clean root can set up enough damage to kill a squishy target, while Final Spark lets you affect a distant fight before you could walk there. Watch side lanes and objective pits between waves, aim along allied control or narrow paths, and account for the cast time. In grouped fights, stay behind your frontline, use Lucent Singularity for damage and sight, and hold Light Binding for the engage or flank. Keep enough distance that a missed bind does not expose you to the enemy's first gap closer.
gamePlan.teamfights: Fight from the back and let Light Binding decide things before damage does. Minions do not stop Q, but the second champion or large monster does, so check whether two frontliners will absorb it before aiming at the carry. Follow a root with Singularity, which detonates automatically on the trapped target, then Final Spark while their movement is predictable. Use Prismatic Barrier through as many allies as possible on its outward and returning path. If the fight starts elsewhere, fire the global laser along allied crowd control rather than waiting to walk into range.

goodAgainst.note: Lux has the longer pick range, but Lulu can still punish with two-angle Glitterlance poke, enemy-cast Help, Pix!, or a planted Whimsy ring. Keep distance, and account for her shield and Wild Growth before committing the laser.

Unbreakable intercepts every hostile projectile from its facing direction, completely negates the first champion damage instance, and then reduces later damage to Braum; it can therefore screen both Binding and the travelling Singularity. Final Spark is a non-projectile laser, so change angles or wait out the shield before committing Q and E, then use the laser through the formation.
Senna wants a slow attrition lane and your burst rotation beats attrition: every soul she walks up to collect risks a root and a full combo her heal cannot recover.

Janna can punish with Zephyr and tornado rather than only disengaging, while Eye of the Storm can absorb poke and empower her carry's attack. Lux has the range advantage, but should not treat Janna's lane tools as purely defensive.

weakAgainst.note: His hook outranges your comfort zone and starts a crowd control chain you have no dash to break, so one landed hook kills you before your shield helps.
Pyke hunts exactly the squishy immobile target you are, and his execute does not care how far ahead your poke put you, so one pick erases a whole lane of work.
Her engage is hard and sticky, poke barely slows it, and once she crashes in the all-in happens whether you want it or not, a fight her kit wins.

Death Sentence reaches the same lane space as Light Binding, Flay punishes Lux after she steps forward, and Dark Passage removes the carry she finally roots. Keep Prismatic Barrier for the hook target, cast Binding at Thresh's recast path rather than fishing blindly, and pressure only while the lantern or hook is unavailable.

One Rocket Grab can start Blitzcrank's knockup-and-silence chain on an immobile Lux. Prismatic Barrier does not prevent the crowd control, but both passes can still absorb damage if aimed through Lux and her carry during the collapse.

gamePlan.overview:
Lux is a support who threatens the lane without walking into the enemy's range. Light Binding passes through minions and only stops early after rooting up to two champions or large monsters, so opponents cannot hide safely inside their wave. Lucent Singularity remains on empty ground for sight, but Lux cannot detonate it manually; it explodes automatically when an enemy enters. Final Spark is a global directional laser that can finish the root combo or influence a fight anywhere on the map.

The plan is simple: land the binding, then collapse. A clean root means a free trade for your ADC, an easy Singularity, and often the laser on top, enough to chunk most supports off the wave. Prismatic Barrier shields your carry through poke and dives, so she protects as well as punishes. The threat of a root off cooldown is half her pressure, and enemies who respect it stop walking up at all.

Her weakness is the usual immobile mage problem. She has no dash or blink, and missing Binding removes her hard control. Singularity's slow and Prismatic Barrier can still help her retreat, but neither stops a hook or knockup that has already connected.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Use Light Binding through the minion wave when an opponent lines up behind it; minions take damage but do not block the root. Because Q deals 90% damage to minions, careless casts can also push the lane or take farm your carry wanted, so choose the line deliberately. Throw Singularity where it can hit the enemy duo, knowing it will explode automatically as soon as either opponent enters the area, and use Prismatic Barrier for the return trade. If Q misses with the enemy jungler nearby, back away until your only reliable peel returns.
gamePlan.midGame: Mid game Lux does not always need to leave lane to swing the map. Final Spark is global, so scan mid, side lanes, and objective pits for allied crowd control, low-health recalls, or predictable paths before firing. Around dragon and herald, place Singularity on an empty entrance for sight; the first enemy to walk in triggers the damage and slow automatically. Binding into laser remains the reliable local pick, while the global option lets you help a distant fight without abandoning your carry or the vision around the next objective.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you decide fights before bodies touch. Stand behind your frontline, hold Binding for the enemy carry or the diver entering your backline, and use the global laser along allied crowd control or narrow objective paths. Watch distant fights between casts because you can contribute without rotating across the map. Prismatic Barrier matters more every minute: send it through your carry and as many teammates as possible so both passes protect the opening exchange.
gamePlan.teamfights: The best opening is a Binding from fog onto a carry or engage tank, followed by Singularity's automatic detonation and Final Spark during the root. Q passes through minions but stops after the second champion or large monster, so do not aim through two frontliners and expect it to reach the backline. If your team is being engaged on, hold Q for the diver and send Prismatic Barrier through your carry instead. A fight happening beyond your screen is still reachable with Final Spark, but aim along allied crowd control because global range does not make the laser unavoidable.

coreItems.name: Liandry's Torment

situationalItems.name: Rylai's Crystal Scepter
situationalItems.note: A slow on every spin and burn tick, so kited targets never quite reach her and fleeing ones never escape.

situationalItems.name: Banshee's Veil

situationalItems.name: Cryptbloom

Choose it when enemies have not built much magic resist, so trading Void Staff's extra damage for more ability haste and an area heal after takedowns is worthwhile.

keystoneRune.name: Phase Rush

keystoneRune.note: Three separate attacks or abilities trigger Phase Rush, compounding the Prance speed from her Q. Use that burst and slow resistance to leave melee range while Dream-Laden Bough keeps burning the target.

primaryRunes.name: Battle Zeal
primaryRunes.desc: While in combat with an enemy champion, gain stacking basic ability damage amplification.
primaryRunes.note: Her passive keeps Lillia in champion combat while she kites, giving Battle Zeal time to stack before later Q and W casts land with the full basic-ability amplification.

primaryRunes.name: Cut Down
primaryRunes.desc: You deal bonus adaptive damage (except true damage) to enemy champions above 60% health.
primaryRunes.note: Cut Down amplifies her magic damage against targets above 60% health, helping her passive and repeated Q casts start melting a healthy frontline immediately; it does not amplify the true-damage edge of Q.

primaryRunes.name: Legend: Bloodline
primaryRunes.desc: Gain permanent omnivamp by taking down champions, monsters, and minions.
primaryRunes.note: Jungle camps stack Bloodline quickly, and its omnivamp turns the repeated Q hits and passive burn into sustain while she clears and kites through long fights.

secondaryRunes.name: Transcendence
secondaryRunes.desc: Gain ability haste, then reduce a basic ability's cooldown after it hits at level 9.
secondaryRunes.note: At level 9, hitting with a basic ability reduces another basic cooldown. Lillia's repeated Q casts keep triggering that loop, bringing W and E back sooner while also rebuilding Prance stacks.

spells.name: Flash
spells.note: Must take. Essential for repositioning, escapes, and aggressive combos.

spells.name: Smite
spells.note: Required for Jungling. Secures objectives and sustains through camp clears.

goodAgainst.note: After your first item, Prance lets you kite Nunu's short-range damage and clear quickly enough to answer his rotations. Apply Dream Dust before he channels Absolute Zero so Lilting Lullaby can interrupt it, but respect that his opening clear and gank tempo are faster than yours.

Blooming Blows movement speed keeps Lillia outside Ixtal's Impact and Impale range while Dream-Laden Bough and Swirlseed stack Dream Dust. Lilting Lullaby then sleeps Skarner before his slow approach can finish the suppression setup.

weakAgainst.note: Rengar is your worst matchup: a burst assassin who leaps from brush onto your squishy frame and deletes you before your burn ever matters. Only items and your sleep ever flip the fight.

Kha'Zix gains isolated Taste Their Fear damage when Lillia paths alone, and Leap reaches her before Blooming Blows has built enough movement speed to kite. Contest with a camp, ward, or teammate nearby to remove isolation, keep Swirlseed for the approach, and use Lilting Lullaby defensively rather than trying to finish a slow solo burn.
Zed's shadow swaps close the gap instantly, and his upfront burst kills you long before your damage over time does any work, so your kite means nothing against him.

gamePlan.overview:
Lillia is a kiting jungler who applies Dream-Laden Bough, builds movement speed through repeated casts, and keeps moving while the burn deals damage. Blooming Blows rewards hitting with the outer edge, while Watch Out! Eep! punishes a target that can be held near its center. Lilting Lullaby can put recently marked enemies to sleep, giving her team a clear follow-up window.

She wins by building into tempo, not by dominating the opening clear. Her first route is ordinary because her damage and movement have not scaled yet, but the first completed item turns repeated area casts into a much faster farming cycle. Her ganks before Lilting Lullaby are real but soft, with movement speed and burn rather than hard lockdown. Once the ultimate and first item are online, she can clear, rotate, and threaten a sleep before slower teams reset their formation.

Her core weakness is the early skirmish. She is squishy, her early single-target damage is a slow burn rather than a punch, and she has no escape beyond running fast. A burst assassin or a sticky early dueler who catches her at scuttle or in her own jungle can delete her before her damage ever ramps.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Lillia's first clear is not especially fast, so prioritize clean camp pulls and preserving health over racing an early farming specialist. Clip camps with Blooming Blows' outer edge, land the center of Watch Out! Eep!, and carry Prance between nearby targets when the route allows it. Contest scuttle only when the matchup and lane priority support you; the clear-speed advantage arrives after the first completed item, not during the opening lap.

Early ganks begin with a long Swirlseed or a Prance-assisted Blooming Blows and rely on Dream Dust pressure rather than hard control. Once Lilting Lullaby is available, apply Dream Dust before casting it. Let a high-damage non-persistent hit, often the center of Watch Out! Eep!, consume the sleep bonus rather than waking the target with the weakest available attack.
gamePlan.midGame:
Objective fights reward Lillia for arriving with Prance stacked and Dream Dust ready to spread. Her ultimate cannot sleep someone merely for walking into the pit; an ability must first apply Dream Dust. Keep Prance stacked and contest when nearby lanes can move, choosing between Herald's immediate tower pressure and progressing toward a Dragon Soul.

Between objectives, hit a side-lane target, cast Lilting Lullaby while Dream Dust is active, and position for the sleep follow-up during the 1.5-second drowsy delay. Counter-jungle when the enemy jungler shows far away, but remember that sleep is unavailable until an ability first hits a champion.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you are a kiting AoE threat who decides fights from the edge of them, not a diver who commits and hopes. Around Baron and dragon your job is to control the area with your speed and your sleep: flip a contested pit by drowsying the enemy frontline as they engage, or peel a diver off your carry by putting the whole dive package to sleep. Power-farm between objectives to keep your damage relevant, because your burn scales with your items and a fed Lillia melts even tanks over the course of a fight. Never throw yourself into the middle of five people; orbit the fight, stack speed, and pick your sleep angle, because an alive kiting Lillia is worth far more than a dead aggressive one.
gamePlan.teamfights: Your teamfight is built around one perfect Lilting Lullaby, so the whole fight is positioning for it. Before you ult, you want your dream dust already on as many enemies as possible, because everyone you have hit gets drowsy and then sleeps, turning one button into a multi-person knockout. Land it on a clustered backline or on the enemy engage and your team collapses on free targets while the burn finishes the work. In a messy fight, use the ult defensively instead: sleep the assassin or bruiser leaping at your carry and you have peeled the dive without trading anyone. The whole time, kite on your speed stacks, spread the Watch Out burn across their team, and stay mobile so nobody pins down the squishy jungler who just decided the fight.

boots.name: Armored Advance

coreItems.name: Force of Nature
