spells.note: Must take. Essential for repositioning, escapes, and aggressive combos.

goodAgainst.note: Tryndamere cannot burst a tank, and your stun plus bite win the long trade against his spin, though his ultimate can deny the kill at the end.
His burst is built for squishy targets and you are not one. Your stun breaks his combo, your bite heals through the dive, and your level three all-in arrives before his items make him scary.
Malphite has poke but no sustain, so your bite out-heals what he takes, and part of your damage is magic his armor does not answer. His ground-targeted charge is the one real threat.

Counter Strike evades the empowered basic attack from Thundering Smash as well as Volibear's normal attacks, so do not waste the stun into it. Sky Splitter and Frenzied Maul still give Volibear tools to trade, but Jax out-scales the duel once his items arrive.

weakAgainst.note: She tumbles out of your charge line, shreds your health while walking backward, and her wall stun ends dives that would kill anyone else.
Mini Gnar kites your charge and pokes from a range you cannot answer, and Mega Gnar has the crowd control to stop your dive, so the stun your lane depends on rarely lands.

Spirit's Refuge blocks the empowered Thundering Smash attack and Volibear's normal attacks. Shen's taunt pauses Thundering Smash while Volibear is immobilized rather than consuming it, but the lost time can still deny the engage and protect Shen's team.
Garen's regen refunds the damage your bite grinds out, his silence cuts your combo the moment you charge in, and his spin hurts enough that he wins the long attrition fight.

gamePlan.overview:
Volibear's lane is built around his level-three all-in. Thundering Smash speeds him toward a visible champion and empowers his next attack to pounce and stun. The first Frenzied Maul on a champion or large monster starts an eight-second Frenzy; a second cast during that window becomes a stronger bite that heals him. Damaging enemies also stacks attack speed, and at five passive stacks his attacks begin chaining bonus magic damage to nearby visible enemies.

His signature trick is his ultimate: a leap that slams down, gives him a big chunk of health, and disables the enemy tower under him. Dives that would kill any other champion are routine for Volibear, so a low enemy hugging their tower is still not safe.

His weaknesses are clear. He is slow between cooldowns, his charge is telegraphed, and ranged kiting leaves him no way to start a fight. Volibear wins by landing the early all-ins and snowballing dives before kiting comps get organized.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Level three is your first real kill window. Place Sky Splitter where the fight will happen, start Thundering Smash so the stun lands near the delayed lightning strike, then cast Frenzied Maul once to begin Frenzy. Stay close enough to cast it again within eight seconds: only that empowered second bite deals increased damage and heals. Enemy immobilization pauses Q rather than cancelling it, but ranged opponents can use that delay to reopen distance. At level five, Stormbringer can disable nearby enemy turrets for a dive.
gamePlan.midGame: Bruiser items plus Stormbringer create a strong dive window, but check the next wave and enemy reinforcements before disabling a turret. Crash first, mark the target with Frenzied Maul, and leap only when the ultimate's landing and bonus health leave a path out. Around the six-minute objectives, Herald is usually the stronger even conversion and Volibear can frontline its narrow entrance. Choose dragon when your composition wants repeated grouped fights toward soul. In either pit, prepare Sky Splitter where the enemy must step and start Thundering Smash before they enter its delayed strike.
gamePlan.lateGame: Clear the Baron side wave early enough to group before Baron or Elder, then choose between frontlining for your carry and diving a reachable backline target. Start Thundering Smash before the engage, but do not cross the whole formation if its movement window will end before contact. Stormbringer can follow a committed target or cross terrain, while its bonus health helps absorb the first response. Keep Frenzied Maul's mark on a target that will remain nearby for the empowered second bite, and reposition if kiting prevents that recast.
gamePlan.teamfights: Pick a reachable target before the fight starts and check whether your carry needs Volibear closer. Thundering Smash stuns through its empowered attack if the target does not evade or block it, while Stormbringer can land behind the frontline or cut off a retreat. Cast Frenzied Maul once to begin Frenzy, place Sky Splitter where the brawl will remain, and stay close enough for the empowered second bite only while allied damage can follow. If the backline is unreachable, use the stun and repeated bite to control the frontline instead of landing alone in the middle.

startingItem.name: Amplifying Tome
startingItem.note: Early ability power for stronger damage and healing. Vladimir has no mana, but cooldowns still limit his rotation and Sanguine Pool spends current health, so his trading is not unrestricted by a resource bar.

boots.name: Spellslinger's Shoes

coreItems.desc: AP engage item with a dash
coreItems.note: A gap closer for a short-range caster. The dash puts him in range of the carry, and the burst opens the drain fight.

coreItems.name: Riftmaker
coreItems.note: Ramping bonus damage and Omnivamp during long fights, and the bonus health feeds straight back into ability power.

coreItems.name: Rabadon's Deathcap
coreItems.note: Multiplies his ability power, which is his damage and, through his Q healing, his sustain.

coreItems.name: Void Staff
coreItems.note: Cuts the magic resist teams stack against him late, so his ultimate-amplified rotation still burns through. Choose it over Cryptbloom when enemies are stacking magic resist and maximum personal damage matters more than ability haste and team healing.

coreItems.note: Haste means more Q casts, and the move speed keeps him moving through fights without spending his pool to reposition.

situationalItems.name: Morellonomicon

situationalItems.name: Oceanid's Trident
situationalItems.note: Build this when the enemy has shields that keep absorbing his sustained damage.

situationalItems.name: Banshee's Veil
situationalItems.note: Build this when the enemy has a binding or silence timed for when his pool is down, which is the pattern that kills him.

situationalItems.name: Zhonya's Hourglass
situationalItems.note: Take this over Rocketbelt when surviving matters more than reaching the carry, since only one item active can be equipped. Buy Seeker's Armguard early for the armor and ability power.

situationalItems.name: Stormsurge
situationalItems.note: His rotation already does enough damage to trigger the mark on a squishy, and the move speed helps a mage with no dash.

situationalItems.name: Cryptbloom
situationalItems.note: The alternative to Void Staff. Less penetration, but the ability haste means more Q casts and the healing on takedown helps his team. Choose it when enemies have not built much magic resist, so trading Void Staff's extra damage for more ability haste and an area heal after takedowns is worthwhile.

keystoneRune.name: Phase Rush
keystoneRune.desc: Hitting an enemy champion with 3 separate attacks or abilities grants movement speed and slow resistance.
keystoneRune.note: His rotation is several quick hits, and the move speed is how a short-range caster disengages once his pool is spent.

primaryRunes.name: Axiom Arcanist
primaryRunes.desc: Empower your spell-focused burst with extra damage and scaling for ability-heavy champions.
primaryRunes.note: He spends health rather than mana, and his ultimate is what amplifies the rotation that follows it, so the ultimate is the part worth raising.

primaryRunes.name: Transcendence
primaryRunes.desc: Gain ability haste, then reduce a basic ability's cooldown after it hits at level 9.
primaryRunes.note: Ability haste means more Q casts, which is his damage and his sustain.

primaryRunes.name: Nimbus Cloak
primaryRunes.desc: After casting a summoner spell, gain movement speed and slow resistance.
primaryRunes.note: Move speed after a summoner spell helps him close the last steps into his short casting range.

secondaryRunes.name: Last Stand
secondaryRunes.desc: Deal more damage to champions while you are low on health.
secondaryRunes.note: He spends fights at low health by design, since his own casts cost him some.

spells.name: Flash
spells.note: Must take. Essential for repositioning, escapes, and aggressive combos.

goodAgainst.note: Vladimir can sustain through Lux's poke and use Sanguine Pool to avoid Light Binding, but Lucent Singularity's automatic detonation and slow plus Prismatic Barrier's two passes still protect her after Q misses. Pool the decisive root, leave E's area, and account for the shield before committing Hemoplague.
Veigar's plan is cage into one-shot, and your pool dodges both halves of it, while your healing shrugs off the poke he farms stacks with. He out-scales most mids, but not you.
Brand's burst hits hard but it is limited, and your health bar refills, so once his rotation is spent you walk him down and he has no escape from it.

Twisted Fate threatens side lanes with Destiny, but his lane trade still depends on a visible Pick a Card windup and he has no dash when Vladimir closes. Hold Sanguine Pool for the Gold Card projectile or jungle follow-up, then use the cooldown window to extend the trade; when he channels Destiny, shove immediately so every roam costs a wave and plates.

weakAgainst.note: Her binding and puddle bully the weak early game your whole plan depends on surviving, and a root timed for when your pool is down pins you for a trade you cannot escape.
Ryze's targeted root and relentless poke chip you faster than your Q heals it back, and he scales right alongside you with a health pool and mana scaling that shrug off your burst.
His magic shield absorbs your burst, his silence shuts off the Q healing that keeps you alive in trades, and once his ultimate is online he out-scales even you.
Swain is the one battlemage who out-sustains you: his drain and ultimate refill health faster than your Q, his root pins you for the combo, and he gets too tanky to burst late.

gamePlan.overview:
Vladimir is a resourceless battlemage who converts health and ability power through Crimson Pact: bonus health grants ability power, while ability power grants bonus health, without those bonuses recursively feeding each other. Transfusion damages and heals, then builds Bloodthirst toward an empowered Crimson Rush cast with extra damage, healing, and a brief movement-speed burst. Sanguine Pool makes him untargetable while he moves, slows and damages enemies beneath him, and heals from that damage; Tides of Blood charges a damaging nova and can still be released after he enters the pool.

Hemoplague is the teamfight multiplier, not a persistent drain. It infects champions in the target area for four seconds, makes them take increased magic damage during the mark, then bursts for damage and heals Vladimir for each infected champion. His game is to survive a vulnerable opening, scale Crimson Pact with health and ability power, and time his charged damage and delayed healing so the enemy cannot finish him between casts.

The cost is that early game. Before items he is squishy, immobile between pool cooldowns, and helpless against the assassins who beat his scaling timer. The pool is one panic button per fight, not an escape plan, so burning it wrong leaves him a slow mage in the open with no way out. Survive the early game and the late game is a completely different story.
gamePlan.earlyGame: The opening phase is purely about survival, so play it that way. Farm at the edge of the wave, soak the poke you cannot avoid, and trade only in short windows where your healing recovers more than their chip takes. Track the enemy jungler constantly, because a short-range mage with one pool and no real escape is the dream gank target, and bad positioning before level five hands the lane away. Do not push just to push: a shoved wave you cannot follow up on walks you into a freeze. Keep your health bar topped up, deny what you can, and remember that every minute you stay even brings the game closer to being yours.
gamePlan.midGame: This is where the scaling pays off. Your first item or two makes your waveclear real, and a cleared wave frees you to leave: shove, then roam to a side lane or river, where your sustained damage and all-in threat make ganks land. With mid priority, set up the dragons and Heralds your team contests, arriving as the body that does not die instead of the one that gets picked. In skirmishes you no longer trade to chip, you trade to win: pour your area damage into the cluster while your healing carries you through their answer. Save the pool for the gank that comes for you, not the first scary thing you see.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you are a diving battlemage, not a true frontliner. Mark as many priority targets as possible with Hemoplague, then land Tides of Blood and Transfusion during its four-second increased-magic-damage window. The detonation damages every infected target and then heals you, with reduced healing from each champion beyond the first, so plan Sanguine Pool or stasis to survive until that delayed heal arrives. Position to reach the carry without throwing your life away, and hold the pool for the lockdown that would end you.
gamePlan.teamfights: Your job is to dive in, apply Hemoplague broadly, and exploit its four-second window with magic damage before the delayed burst and heal. Charge Tides of Blood as you enter, and use Sanguine Pool to avoid a decisive response; if Tides was already charging, it can still be released from the pool. Crimson Rush's meter depletes more slowly while charging Tides, pooled, or in stasis, so those states can preserve the empowered Transfusion timing rather than waste it. Pick an angle that reaches the backline without stranding you after Pool ends.

startingItem.name: Amplifying Tome
startingItem.note: Early ability power for Hextech Ray, his safest way to clear and pressure the wave while collecting Hex Fragments.

boots.name: Spellslinger's Shoes
boots.note: Magic penetration keeps his laser and storm relevant before his items arrive.

coreItems.name: Blackfire Torch
coreItems.note: His laser and storm keep the burn applied on everything they touch, so the stacking bonus sits near its cap.

coreItems.name: Liandry's Torment

gamePlan.overview:
Viktor is a scaling control mage whose power comes from both gold and Glorious Evolution. Minions and monsters grant Hex Fragments when Viktor kills them, with siege minions, super minions, epic monsters, and champion takedowns granting more. Every 100 fragments lets him upgrade one basic ability; after all three are upgraded, Arcane Storm can evolve too. Hextech Ray clears and pokes along a chosen line, Gravity Field repeatedly slows before stunning on its third stack, and Siphon Power damages a target, shields Viktor, and empowers his next attack. Its upgrade also grants movement speed and a stronger shield.

His win condition is patience with a payoff. Shove the wave with Hextech Ray, secure last hits for fragments, and turn priority into river vision and objectives. Champion takedowns accelerate his evolution sharply, so a safe rotation can be worth more than another isolated wave. You are building toward upgraded spells and items that make later skirmishes lopsided.

The cost is mobility. Viktor has no dash and no blink, only a little speed from his shield, so when an assassin gets on top of him the gravity field is his one real answer, and if they dodge it he is a stationary mage in a bad spot. Laners who out-tempo his early game make him pay for every minute before his spike.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Play around Hextech Ray's line: fire it through the wave and enemy champion when their positioning allows, but secure the minion kills rather than sacrificing fragments for careless poke. Use Siphon Power's shield and empowered non-projectile attack for short trades. Save Gravity Field for ganks or a committed melee opponent, because targets need three field stacks before the stun triggers. In an aggressive matchup, farm the first few levels and accept that your evolution arrives later than their first combat spike.
gamePlan.midGame: This is where the patience pays. Upgraded Hextech Ray adds a delayed explosion along its path, sharply improving waveclear and zone damage; that speed is map pressure. Shove, then walk to river to help your jungler or set vision around Dragon and Herald before your team commits. In skirmishes around the pit, place Gravity Field on a chokepoint where enemies cannot leave before its third stack, then line Hextech Ray through the trapped group. Champion takedowns grant a large fragment burst, so successful rotations accelerate the next upgrade.
gamePlan.lateGame: This is the version of Viktor every other phase was building toward. Upgraded Hextech Ray hits twice, upgraded Gravity Field makes his other basic abilities and Arcane Storm's initial hit slow, and upgraded Arcane Storm grows and lasts longer when champions it damaged are taken down. The storm initially follows the nearest enemy champion automatically, but after you manually redirect it, it travels to that location rather than resuming automatic pursuit. Play as a backline control mage and use vision and positioning so the enemy never gets a clean line to you.
gamePlan.teamfights: Your job is to melt the enemy from the second row and lock down their approach. Place Gravity Field on a choke or committed group so its repeated slow stacks can reach the third-stack stun, then cast Arcane Storm where its initial hit can also disrupt an enemy channel. Let the storm track the nearest champion when that behavior is useful; recast only when you deliberately want to redirect it, because it stops automatically following afterward. Keep Gravity Field back if a diver is hunting you, and weave Siphon Power's empowered attack when it is safe enough to use the shield and movement-speed upgrade.

gamePlan.overview:
Yasuo is a mid laner who uses enemy units as a chain of targeted dashes. Sweeping Blade travels a fixed distance through its target and cannot be used on that same unit again for several seconds, so a minion wave provides routes only when those individual targets are still available. Wind Wall blocks hostile non-turret projectiles that collide with it, not ground zones, beams, or every spell in a mage's kit.

Steel Tempest gains Gathering Storm only when it hits an enemy; after two stacks, its next cast becomes a knockup whirlwind. Casting it during Sweeping Blade instead creates a circular strike at the dash endpoint. Last Breath requires a nearby airborne enemy champion, blinks Yasuo to the far side, catches nearby airborne champions, grants maximum Flow, and resets his tornado stacks. Its 15-second follow-up grants armor penetration only to Yasuo's critical-strike damage.

The catch is the early game. A pre-item Yasuo is a melee champion with a small health bar and limited threat, and the whole mid pool knows that window is the time to make him miserable. If he falls behind before his shield and crit items mature, he spends the game with no way to carry.
gamePlan.earlyGame: The first few levels are about staying even, not making plays. Last-hit with Steel Tempest, let it stack toward the tornado, and only trade when you can land the knockup and dash out before the answer comes; you cannot dash through the same target twice in a row, and good mids will bait it. Wind Wall is your matchup-bending trick: one well-timed wall erases the poke spell or root the enemy's whole lane is built around, so save it for the cast that matters instead of throwing it at minions. Check the enemy jungler before extending, because you have no escape without a minion to dash through, and dying to a gank before your items is how Yasuo games are lost. Push only when you plan to follow with a roam or tower poke; otherwise hold the wave near the middle and farm toward your spike.
gamePlan.midGame: Two items in, the lane flips. Tornado into ultimate now kills most squishy mids outright, side-lane duels tilt your way, and the wave becomes a tool for roams instead of a chore. Shove when you have priority and look across the river: your dashes make you one of the better roaming mids once you have a wave to dash through, and a knockup on a distracted carry usually ends in a kill. Use that same priority to crash the wave before scuttle fights and contests at dragon or Herald, where one Wind Wall across their poke or one tornado into a clump swings the skirmish before it starts. This window is where Yasuo players earn the win, so treat tempo and picks as the job rather than farming a static lane.
gamePlan.lateGame: By late game you are a crit duelist with a teleporting finisher. Take a side lane when the map allows: few mids win a straight 1v1 against two or three crit items, and your dashes make you hard to gank. In grouped fights, be patient: wait for a knockup, yours or a teammate's, then ultimate onto the airborne priority target and shred them before their team can peel. Save Wind Wall for the projectile that decides the fight, whether that is the enemy artillery's big spell or their engage tool, and treat it as a fight-winning cooldown rather than poke insurance. Dashing into all five enemies at once has ended more Yasuo games than any counter pick, so pick entries that have an exit.
gamePlan.teamfights: Hunt the knockup and let everything else follow it. Your own whirlwind or circular dash-Q can supply it, while an ally's airborne effect can set up a cleaner Last Breath. The ultimate generates maximum Flow for the next champion or monster hit, resets Gathering Storm, and gives Yasuo's critical strikes armor penetration for 15 seconds, so the melee follow-up is the payoff rather than the cast being an execute. Wind Wall the decisive projectile and preserve an unused dash target for the exit.

gamePlan.overview:
Yasuo is a melee carry whose critical-strike chance from other sources is doubled. Excess critical chance above 100% converts to bonus attack damage, while movement builds Flow; at full Flow, taking champion or monster damage consumes it for a short shield. Sweeping Blade targets enemy units and cannot reuse the same target for several seconds, so minion waves provide planned routes rather than unlimited free dashes. Wind Wall blocks hostile non-turret projectiles that collide with it.

Steel Tempest gains a stack only when it hits an enemy; after two stacks, the next cast launches a knockup whirlwind. Casting it during Sweeping Blade produces a circular strike at the dash endpoint instead. Last Breath requires a nearby airborne enemy champion, catches nearby airborne champions, generates maximum Flow, resets Gathering Storm, and grants 15 seconds of armor penetration specifically to Yasuo's critical-strike damage.

The early game is the price. Before items Yasuo is a squishy melee who badly needs gold, and the lane knows it. The whole pick is a bet that he survives long enough for his crit items to take over.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Keep the wave in a position that gives Sweeping Blade several safe routes. Farm with Mortal Steel, prepare the whirlwind on minions, and trade only when you can dash through the opponent and still have a different unit for the exit. Against ranged matchups, Wind Wall should stop the spell that enables their full trade rather than a minor poke cast. Against melee bruisers, use Flow and spacing to absorb one response, then leave before their longer all-in begins. Your first items matter more than forcing an early kill.
gamePlan.midGame: With critical-strike items and Last Breath available, Yasuo can pressure the side lane and threaten river skirmishes. Crash before rotating to Herald, and prefer fights near a minion wave or jungle camp where Sweeping Blade has several legal targets. Use your whirlwind or an ally's knockup to reach a priority champion, then decide whether the armor penetration window is worth continuing the chase. Save Wind Wall for the projectile that controls or bursts you, and avoid long side-lane pushes when the next objective is already spawning.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game, push a side wave only when you can return before Baron or Elder is contested. In fights, wait for your whirlwind, circular dash-Q, or an ally's knockup to lift a target worth reaching. Last Breath grants maximum Flow and 15 seconds of armor penetration for critical strikes, but the blink can still place you inside the enemy team with no exit. Track which units remain eligible for Sweeping Blade, wall the projectile that matters most, and attack the frontline when diving the carry would end your damage immediately.
gamePlan.teamfights: Play around the safest useful knockup. Your own whirlwind or circular dash-Q can start the sequence, while allied airborne control often lets you enter without spending every movement option. Last Breath extends the airborne window, fills Flow, resets Mortal Steel's stacks, and empowers subsequent critical strikes with armor penetration. Place Wind Wall between the enemy backline and the fight, then preserve an eligible Sweeping Blade target for repositioning. If no safe backline entry appears, protect your carry and damage the closest target until one does.

gamePlan.overview:
Zed is the jungle assassin who farms in two places at once. His shadows throw a second set of shurikens from another angle, so camps take Q from two sides, his W swap doubles as a repositioning tool, and his ultimate marks a target for a delayed hit that deals huge damage.

He wins by turning farm into kills. Early on he is average: his clear is fine but not fast, and his squishy melee frame has no hard crowd control. The payoff comes from ganks and dives. A shadow onto a lane lets him close the gap, slow, and chunk with energized shurikens, and once his ultimate is up he simply kills the first overextended carry he reaches. From there it is the usual assassin snowball: pick someone off, take the tempo, repeat before the map recovers.

Zed has no hard crowd control, and the shadow swap used to enter may also be his safest exit. Strong early duelists can deny Scuttle or invade before his damage spikes, while reliable lockdown can catch him before he returns to a shadow. A tank standing in front of the intended target also makes his single-target burst much harder to apply.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Your first clear is about clean overlap. Place Living Shadow so Zed and the copy can hit the camp with the same Shuriken and restore energy, without forcing the missile through another unit first. Shadow Slash adds damage, but monsters do not trigger the champion-only Living Shadow cooldown reduction. Reach level five with enough tempo to punish an overextended lane rather than forcing an early duel without hard crowd control.

Clear toward the lane with the best setup, but do not force a gank when the target is healthy and protected by the wave. Contest Scuttle only with enough health, cooldowns, and nearby lane priority to survive the duel. If the enemy jungler controls one crab, take the other or return to camps instead of forcing a losing river fight. Track the opposing route and ward your entrances so an invade does not remove the farm Zed needs for level five.
gamePlan.midGame:
Zed gains more from a pick before the objective than from standing in the pit during a fair contest. Watch the side lanes for a carry who pushed up without vision and collapse on them, then take the objective while their team is down a body. Contest when your team is ahead; in an even game take Herald, since your peak is now and a tower cashes it in.

Between objectives, counter-jungling works well, because you out-duel a lot of farmers in their own jungle and a swap gets you out before help arrives. Keep an eye on the enemy jungler's position, though: a Zed who dives into a waiting counter-gank hands the lead back in one trade.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you are a pick threat, not a brawler. Your job is to find the enemy carry and kill them, which means flanking from fog, waiting until your swap and ultimate are both up, and committing when their backline is actually reachable. Group with your team but fight from the edges: walking through the enemy frontline gets you locked down and bursted, while a clean flank puts your shadow on the target that matters. Baron and dragon fights are where your picks matter most, so hold your engage for the carry instead of wasting it on the frontline, and let your own tanks create the moment of chaos you need. An alive Zed who kills one carry per fight wins the game; a dead Zed who dove the tank wasted his ultimate.
gamePlan.teamfights: Choose the target and exit shadow before entering. Approach from a side angle, apply Death Mark when the carry has spent a defensive tool, and land the energized basic attack plus abilities before swapping back. If tanks block every route, wait for the formation to separate or help damage the nearest target. Do not chase a second takedown when the return shadow is about to expire or the enemy control remains available.

Later, Kassadin cannot remove or dodge a Death Mark already applied, but repeated blinks can avoid the follow-up damage that would feed its detonation while his magic shield absorbs part of your rotation.

Force Chronobreak with shadow poke before committing Death Mark, keep a shadow away from his convergence zone, and disengage if the rewind is still available.

Ring of Frost can root you before a shadow swap. Lissandra's self-cast ultimate does not cleanse Death Mark, but its stasis makes her invulnerable; if she times that invulnerability over the detonation, the burst deals no damage.
His ultimate heals through your Death Mark burst faster than you deal it, his root pins your shadow swap, and his stacked fragments make him too tanky to delete.

gamePlan.overview:
Zed is an energy assassin whose shadows mimic Razor Shuriken and Shadow Slash regardless of range. If Zed and one or more shadows hit the same target with the same ability cast, Living Shadow restores energy once for that cast, so overlapping angles sustain the rotation as well as adding damage. Energy can still run out when those overlaps miss. Death Mark briefly makes Zed untargetable, carries him beyond the selected champion, and marks them for 2.8 seconds. Its shadow appears at Zed's original casting position, not behind the target, giving him a possible swap back after he reappears.

His lane plan is pressure plus patience. He shoves with his spinning blades, pokes with shurikens thrown through a shadow, and waits for the wave to set up a clean ultimate window. Once it is online he stops being a laner and becomes a roaming threat: a Zed with priority and a shadow ready is two lanes the enemy has to play scared in.

The catch is that he is melee, squishy, and spends his escape to start his damage. His shadows are his dash, his poke, and his way out on the same buttons, so the moment they are on cooldown he has nothing left and any crowd control ends him. Champions who survive the burst window or answer his all-in with a stun turn his best play into his death, and a Zed who falls behind never scales into the carry he wanted to be.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Read their range first, not their health bar. Against immobile mages, throw Razor Shuriken through a Living Shadow so both Zed and the shadow threaten the same target, then add Shadow Slash when they are in range. Your first real spike is when the full kit is online, but place Living Shadow with both the damage angle and the possible swap in mind before committing.
gamePlan.midGame: This is your window, and it closes if you sit in it. Shove the wave, then leave: with your ultimate up and a shadow ready, you threaten every lane that is not watching the river. Help your jungler at scuttle, set up a pick before dragon or herald, and walk into a side lane the moment the enemy mid recalls or shoves under your tower. The math is simple: one roam that lands a kill puts two lanes ahead and an objective on a timer. Track the enemy mid's wave so you know whether following you costs them a tower or nothing, and never give up mid priority for a roam that was never going to connect.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you play like a pick assassin, not a brawler. Walking into a teamfight head-on kills you instantly, so your job is to find the one target the fight cannot afford to lose and remove them. Hold your ultimate for their carry, mark them from an angle their frontline cannot peel, and collect the burst before the support's crowd control finds you. Your damage is still real, but you no longer beat a full-build marksman in a straight fight, so the skill is target selection and exit timing. A Zed who kills the right person and lives is worth far more than one who dove the tank and respawned.
gamePlan.teamfights: Pick your target before anyone casts a spell. Death Mark stores a portion of the pre-mitigation physical and magic damage dealt by Zed and his shadows during its window, then detonates as physical damage. Place Living Shadow to create overlapping Shuriken angles and preserve a swap, while remembering the ultimate's own shadow remains at the original cast position. If the enemy is too clumped or well peeled, threaten from the side instead of spending both exits into fresh control.

gamePlan.overview:
Yone fights with two swords and a spirit form. Soul Unbound dashes him forward for up to five seconds while leaving an untargetable body at a fixed return point. Damage dealt to enemy champions during the form stores a portion on each marked target; when Yone returns, every mark is consumed for true damage. The return path itself does not damage enemies, and the fixed endpoint can be camped even though the body cannot be attacked.

His attacks alternate between a physical strike and an Azakana strike split evenly between physical and magic damage. Mortal Steel remains physical, while Spirit Cleave and Fate Sealed deal equal physical and magic portions; Soul Unbound repeats part of post-mitigation champion damage as true damage on return. Spirit Cleave grants a short shield when it hits, not healing or sustain.

His early game is weak and squishy, and every lane bully plans around it. Yone games are about surviving that phase, then taking over with a kit that scales into one of the most flexible divers in the game.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Accept a rough early game. Farm with Mortal Steel and land two casts on enemies to prepare the third-cast dash and knockup. Spirit Cleave shields only when it hits an enemy, with a larger shield for hitting champions. Place Soul Unbound's body in a safe location: it cannot be attacked, but Yone must return there and enemies can prepare crowd control around it. Against bullies, give up ground and take what farm you can.
gamePlan.midGame: Crash the Baron wave before moving to Herald, then prepare Mortal Steel stacks on the remaining minions or a safe target. Start Soul Unbound from a protected return point and use the movement speed, knockup, and attacks to mark the champion with stored damage. Recast to return with displacement immunity and trigger the mark; no enemy needs to stand in the return path. Take side-lane duels only when the body cannot be surrounded and leave enough time to group for the next objective.
gamePlan.lateGame: Push the side wave only when Yone can return before Baron or Elder vision is contested. Start Soul Unbound from a protected point and check which enemies can wait at the body. Use Fate Sealed when its line reaches an important target or several grouped enemies, then return before the enemy collapses on the fixed position. Soul Unbound returns automatically after five seconds, although control that prevents movement or casting can delay the recast.
gamePlan.teamfights: Enter from the flank and leave on time. Fate Sealed briefly stuns targets in its line before the delayed gust damages, pulls, and knocks them up; it does not simply hold them airborne for the whole sequence. Spirit Form is the damage window, and the stored true damage triggers against each marked champion when Yone returns, regardless of the path he takes back. If their crowd control is still available, wait or use Mercurial Scimitar to restore a delayed recast when the disable is removable.

gamePlan.overview:
Yone is a melee skirmisher with alternating swords and a fixed-return spirit form. Mortal Steel gains a stack when it hits an enemy; after two stacks, the next cast dashes and launches a whirlwind that knocks up. Soul Unbound dashes Yone forward for up to five seconds while leaving an untargetable body behind. Damage dealt to enemy champions stores a portion on each marked target, then the return consumes those marks for true damage; the return path itself deals no damage.

His attacks alternate between a physical Steel Sword hit and an Azakana hit split between physical and magic damage. Spirit Cleave and Fate Sealed also deal equal physical and magic portions, while Mortal Steel remains physical. Fate Sealed first knocks down and stuns enemies in its line, blinks Yone beyond the last champion hit or to maximum range, then a delayed gust pulls marked enemies toward him and knocks them up.

The catch is hard crowd control and a thin health bar. With both dashes spent he is a melee champion stranded in the open, and a root, taunt, or fear can catch the path he committed to. Control mages can punish the return point from Soul Unbound, so Yone must track their main disable before using the spirit form aggressively.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Trade in short bursts without a mana or energy cost. Land two Mortal Steel casts on enemies to prepare its dash-knockup, then place Soul Unbound's body somewhere safe before using the spirit form's movement speed to reach the target. Spirit Cleave shields only if it hits an enemy, with a larger shield for champions hit. Against control mids, wait for a clean window: Soul Unbound does not dodge their key spell, and control that prevents movement or casting can delay the return.
gamePlan.midGame: Your first item turns even trades into winning ones, and that is the signal to play for the map instead of the wave. Crash the wave and walk: a roam where your knockup catches an overextended carry is worth more than the minions you left behind, and few mids contest scuttle or a face-checking jungler as well as a Yone with both dashes up. Hold mid priority and you decide who shows up to the first dragon and herald fights, since a champion who can lunge in twice and teleport back out is exactly who you want at a contested pit. When nothing is happening, shove a side lane, apply the split pressure your mobility lets you survive, and rotate back the moment the map needs you.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you stop being a lane bully and become a problem the enemy plans around. Fate Sealed always commits Yone forward; to beyond the last champion hit, or to maximum range if it hits none. Soul Unbound is what returns him to a prior point, so establish that point safely before using the ultimate as an entry. Check the enemy's hard crowd control before committing, because a disable can hold the active spirit and delay its recast even when the five-second timer expires.
gamePlan.teamfights: Decide who you want dead before the fight starts. The clean opening is a prepared third Mortal Steel or Soul Unbound from a flank into Fate Sealed's stun, pull, and knockup. Fate Sealed carries Yone forward but does not provide a way home; only Soul Unbound returns him to its fixed body. The abandoned body cannot be attacked, but its location is visible and enemies can wait there. Recast when the job is done, and remember that the stored true damage is dealt directly to each marked champion rather than along the return path.

gamePlan.overview:
Warwick is a duelist whose kit tracks wounded enemies and runs them down. His passive heals him with every attack and heals more against low targets, his Q bites and drains harder the lower the enemy is, and his W shows him wounded champions across the map and speeds him toward them. Few junglers threaten a half-health target like he does.

He wins by ganking constantly and never losing a long fight. His clear is quick, and his ultimate is a long leap that suppresses a target while his laner walks up for the kill. He is not a burst assassin or a five-man frontline: he isolates one enemy, locks them down, and drains them out before help arrives.

His weak spot is the early game. Before items his ganks are ordinary, his pre-five pickoff relies on a short fear, and any hard crowd control cancels his ultimate mid-leap. Burst him before his healing matters and he becomes a slow melee with no kill threat.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Use Eternal Hunger and Jaws of the Beast to stay healthy while clearing, but let Blood Hunt change the route when a nearby enemy becomes genuinely vulnerable. A wounded, overextended laner can be worth visiting before the full clear; a low-health icon under their own turret is not. Hold Jaws to follow movement and carry yourself behind the target, then fear them back toward your ally with Primal Howl.

Do not recast Howl immediately unless the faster fear matters more than keeping its damage reduction. At scuttle, Warwick can absorb a trade and heal through it, but crowd control and enemy lane priority still beat sustain. Infinite Duress improves your reach at level five, while the early game remains a balance between efficient camps and finishing only the blood trails that lead to real kills.
gamePlan.midGame:
Warwick contests early objectives through sustain and the threat of punishing whoever drops low. Take those fights when your team is ahead. In an even game take Herald and give the dragon up, unless your team is happy to keep fighting for soul, which suits your sustain better than most.

Between objectives Blood Hunt shows trails to enemy champions below half health anywhere on the map. Follow the trail, but remember the movement bonus drops on entering champion combat before rebuilding; use the active to mark the nearest champion for eight seconds when no one is naturally wounded. Trade camps aggressively and use the chase speed to arrive at fights, without assuming it remains at full strength once combat begins.
gamePlan.lateGame: Warwick stays useful late as a diver and pick threat, not as the frontliner who eats the engage. Blood hunt still finds anyone caught alone near Baron or a side lane, and your leap removes them from the map. You also remain a real 1v1 threat even against scaled duelists, so you can punish a split push or hold a flank when the teams spread out. Watch for enemy anti-heal: once their carry buys it your drain loses most of its value, so fight around that item and pick targets who cannot answer your sustain instead of face-tanking a fed marksman. Save your ultimate for the carry that actually needs to die, not the first body you see.
gamePlan.teamfights: Your job is to reach the back line and stay there, not to trade with their tank. Wait for the engage to commit, then leap your ultimate onto their carry and suppress them out of the fight while your team collapses; a clean ult usually kills before they can flash or get peeled. If their front line blocks the path, hold the leap rather than spending it on a body you do not want, and let your sustain keep you alive until a real opening appears. Your passive healing lets you dive through poke and come out fine, so stay in their backline's face and force them to keep watching you. One good suppression on the right target usually decides the fight, so patience with that button beats using it early.

Attached Yuumi is not a separate target for Lux's spells, but the host can still be rooted through minions, slowed by Lucent Singularity's automatic detonation, and hit by the global Final Spark. Shield before the combo and avoid detaching where Light Binding can catch Yuumi herself.

Dark Binding cannot select an attached Yuumi, so Morgana usually has to hit the host. Black Shield absorbs Prowling Projectile's magic damage and prevents its slow while the shield holds, and its crowd-control immunity also prevents Final Chapter's stacking slows; it does not stop Zoomies or Yuumi's healing.

Seraphine's line and area spells can still hit Yuumi's host, but attached Yuumi is not a separate target for them. Shield the host through the poke and steer Prowling Projectile around the wave while Seraphine's long control cooldowns are down.

Braum can block Prowling Projectile with Unbreakable and punish your host with Concussive Blows, so the lane is not free. Yuumi's advantage is that Braum cannot directly target her while attached and must break through the host's Zoomies shield and periodic healing.

weakAgainst.note: Leona chains stun after root onto your carry and the burst lands before your heal catches up. Every second you spend detached is also a free engage onto a cat with no escape.
Nautilus drags your carry out of position with his hook, and the rest of his kit roots them in place long enough to die through any shield you stack. You cannot peel a chain of crowd control.
One hook ends it: he pulls your carry out from under your protection and you ride along into a fight you both lose. The threat also stops you from detaching to poke.
He never needs to hit you, because he hits the champion you live in: a hook on your host is a hook on you, and his flay drags both of you out of position.

Headbutt into Pulverize locks down your host and carries attached Yuumi into the same bad position. Unbreakable Will cleanses crowd control when Alistar casts it and grants damage reduction, but it does not make him permanently crowd-control immune; stack new Final Chapter slows after the cleanse if he keeps chasing.

gamePlan.overview:
Yuumi spends most of the game attached to an ally and untargetable, except to turrets and projectiles already inbound when she attaches. From the host's position she steers Prowling Projectile, casts Zoomies to grant the host a shield and attack speed, and channels Final Chapter through the fight. Zoomies no longer heals in the current Wild Rift kit: her healing comes from the periodic Feline Friendship trigger and from Final Chapter's waves.

Her Dragon-lane plan revolves around Friendship. While Yuumi is attached, that ally gains two permanent Friendship stacks for killing champions or minions; the ally with the most becomes her Best Friend, and Yuumi's abilities gain extra effects while attached to them. Norra is the special exception: she gains no stacks but is automatically treated as Best Friend. An attached Q that flies for at least 0.75 seconds gains damage and a slow, and hitting a champion gives the Best Friend bonus magic damage on-hit.

Yuumi is vulnerable whenever she detaches without a nearby ally. Crowd control can interrupt the attach dash, and You and Me! has an eight-second cooldown early that falls to four seconds at its next rank and disappears at max rank. A careless passive attack or ward attempt can still expose her. Her lane pressure also depends heavily on the host's positioning and ability to use her buffs.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Your early lane is about safely building Friendship with the carry who is taking minions. Stay attached to steer Q: its attached bonus powers up after 0.75 seconds in flight. When Feline Friendship is ready, Yuumi's next attack gains range, becomes non-projectile, and heals her on hitting a champion; an ability hit can trigger it too. Attach within four seconds so the anchor receives the same heal. Use Zoomies before damage lands, and respect the attach dash: immobilization, grounding, or polymorph can knock it down while You and Me! is still on its early eight-second cooldown.
gamePlan.midGame: This is where your value ramps up. Once your ADC has items, Zoomies turns their trades with a shield, attack speed, and movement speed while attached Q adds poke and a temporary Best Friend on-hit buff. Moving to a new fed ally does not instantly make them Best Friend; Friendship is accumulated while attached to their kills, except that Norra is always treated as Best Friend. Around Dragon, aim Final Chapter through both teams so its seven waves heal allies, convert excess healing into a shield, and stack up to a 70% slow on enemies. Hitting an allied champion with Final Chapter can also trigger a ready Feline Friendship heal.
gamePlan.lateGame: Late game you are an extension of your Best Friend. Keep Zoomies available for the shield and attack-speed window, land a long-flight Q to activate their bonus on-hit magic damage, and steer Final Chapter across the dive. The waves do not root, but repeated hits stack their slow while healing allies. Pick hosts with the Friendship system in mind: changing anchors is easy, but the Best Friend bonuses remain tied to whoever has accumulated the most stacks.
gamePlan.teamfights: Start attached to the carry whose Friendship and damage make them your best host. Use Zoomies for its shield before burst lands and its attack speed during their damage window. Prowling Projectile is empowered by staying attached and keeping it in flight for 0.75 seconds, so do not detach to cast it. Final Chapter can be steered while attached; line its seven waves through allies for healing and through divers for stacking slows. Detach only for a safe passive attack, a ward, or a deliberate host swap, because losing the anchor can leave Yuumi exposed.

goodAgainst.note: You both scale, but your hybrid on-hit ramp out-duels her rockets in every extended 2v2, and your speed burst slips the chompers she needs to peel you off her immobile frame.
His early game is as quiet as yours, but your speed burst and slow win the even trades his immobile frame cannot answer. You both scale, and you are the one who can walk away.
Her Spell Shield eats one spell, but your damage is a hundred autos it cannot answer, so your ramp wins every long trade her waveclear tempo keeps starting.

weakAgainst.note: Draven's axes out-hit your entire early game, and your ramp never matters in a trade that ends in two rotations. At even farm, your late game takes over once his strong phase passes.

Caitlyn's basic-attack range and Yordle Snap Traps punish every step Yunara takes toward early farm, while 90 Caliber Net preserves that spacing if Yunara accelerates at her. Use Arc of Judgment to slow from outside the trap line, keep Kanmei's Steps for the net retreat, and accept early farm losses until Cultivation of Spirit can win the longer damage race.

gamePlan.overview:
Yunara is a marksman built around attack speed and critical strikes. Vow of the First Lands adds magic damage to critical strikes. Cultivation of Spirit passively adds magic damage on-hit; while its active is unavailable, attacks build Unleash up to six stacks and refresh its duration. Activating it consumes Unleash for five seconds of attack speed, additional on-hit magic damage, and physical splash around the primary target. If the attack crits, the splash crits too.

Arc of Judgment sends a spinning prayer bead that heavily slows on the initial hit, then lingers and repeatedly damages nearby enemies at its endpoint. Kanmei's Steps grants movement speed and ghosting, with a larger speed boost while moving toward a nearby visible enemy champion. It is not a dash until Transcend One's Self upgrades it to Untouchable Shadow.

The cost is the usual hyper-carry package: average early trades, one speed burst as her entire escape plan, and a lane that denies her farm delays the only part of her game that matters.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Farm like the late game depends on it, because it does. Take what the wave offers, let your support handle the aggression, and keep your prayer bead between you and the enemy carry so every trade happens across a slow. Your on-hit damage makes short, even trades better than they look, but do not chase them: your speed burst is your only way out, and spending it to win a trade is how Yunaras die to the next gank. Track the enemy jungler before you cross river, and treat every level as a step toward the fights you actually win.
gamePlan.midGame: Your first items turn skirmishes into trades the enemy keeps losing. Group for dragons, hold the edge of the fight, and let your ramp decide the standoffs around the pit. The W slow both starts and refuses fights: drop it on the choke when you want the enemy to come through, or behind you when you need them to stop. Save the speed burst for the one diver every enemy comp sends at you. A Yunara who survives the engage usually wins the fight that follows.
gamePlan.lateGame: You are the win condition now, and everyone knows it. Transcend One's Self lasts 15 seconds and does not grant general attack range. It automatically activates Cultivation of Spirit, changes Arc of Judgment into a long slowing laser, and changes Kanmei's Steps into a directional dash; basic abilities cost no mana during the state. Do not walk first through fog, and use the empowered dash to preserve attack time rather than assuming the ultimate itself makes you safe.
gamePlan.teamfights: Attack whatever the fight puts in range and trust your sustained damage. Entering Transcendent State automatically activates Q, reduces Arc of Ruin's remaining cooldown sharply, and refreshes E as it becomes Untouchable Shadow; leaving the state adjusts those cooldowns again. Use Kanmei's Steps before the ultimate when safe, then preserve the refreshed dash for the enemy's engage. Arc of Ruin is a laser, not a lingering prayer bead, and the ultimate does not extend basic-attack range.

goodAgainst.note: Master Yi needs uninterrupted attacks, but he is untargetable during Alpha Strike. Hold Vault Breaker or your ultimate until he reappears, then chain the knockups before he can resume attacking.
Nidalee wants to poke from range, but your Q closes the gap straight through her spears, and she has no bulk to survive once the brawl starts.
Zed's whole identity is his shadow escape, and your point-and-click ult ignores it, pinning him mid-combo before the swap can pull him to safety.

weakAgainst.note: Nunu's knockup interrupts your Vault Breaker the instant you commit, his bulk shrugs off your burst, and he peels the carry you actually wanted, so your single-target dive gets nothing.
Taliyah shoves you back out of your own engage with Seismic Shove, an empowered Threaded Volley from Worked Ground can slow your approach, and her poke chunks you before Vault Breaker connects.
Rammus turns your engage against you: his taunt locks you onto him while Defensive Ball Curl reflects the autos Denting Blows stack, and your physical burst does little into his armor.

gamePlan.overview:
Vi is a jungler built to reach and delete the enemy carry. Her charged Q closes gaps and knocks a target back, her passive shreds armor and adds attack speed, Blast Shield lets her brawl without backing off, and her ultimate is a point-and-click lock that picks an enemy up and cannot be stopped by dashes.

She is a tempo diver with a fast clear, especially during the opening routes. Relentless Force cuts through groups while Denting Blows speeds up attacks on the large monster, so she can finish camps quickly and turn that timing into a Q knockup or an early objective. She wins by converting the clear lead into repeat pressure and removing the enemy carry from later fights.

Her weakness is the commitment. Vault Breaker is usually her way in, Cease and Desist carries her deep toward its target, and neither leaves an escape for the fight that follows. Teams with strong peel can protect the carry, control Vi after she arrives, and punish an engage that her allies cannot immediately follow.
gamePlan.earlyGame:
Vi clears quickly from the opening route: Relentless Force damages the smaller monsters together, while repeated attacks trigger Denting Blows on the large target. Use that speed to reach a gank, river contest, or level-five timing before a slower jungler. After three camps, a charged Vault Breaker can already punish an overextended target; otherwise finish the route and preserve the tempo lead.

Vi can fight for scuttle, but charging Vault Breaker in vision tells the opponent exactly how to dodge or interrupt you. Use terrain and brush to hide the wind-up, activate Blast Shield after building stacks to absorb the return trade, and keep enough information on nearby lanes before following a missed Q into the river. Cease and Desist later guarantees the engage; it does not make the earlier pressure irrelevant.
gamePlan.midGame:
Vi enters the first objective fights with a reliable way to lock the enemy jungler or punish a carry who steps forward. Contesting you means fighting someone who can lock onto whoever flinches, so take those fights when your team is ahead on early skirmishes. In an even game take Herald and trade the dragon away, since your pressure converts a tower quickly, and leave soul to a comp built to hold five on fives.

Between objectives, crash a wave, mark a target, and turn every cross-map gank into a numbers lead. This is also your window to invade a slower jungler, since your dueling beats most farm-and-scale picks and your ultimate locks on, so walking away is not the answer.
gamePlan.lateGame: Group before Baron and hold a flank that keeps allies within follow-up range. Use Cease and Desist on a carry only when the path will not drag Vi through the entire enemy formation without support. If the backline is protected, use Vault Breaker and the ultimate to stop a diver or lock the nearest high-damage target. Clear vision with the team and punish an isolated face-check instead of revealing the engage from the front.
gamePlan.teamfights: Your fight is decided before it starts: pick the target, then get into lock-on range of it. The best case is an ultimate onto their carry that brings you to them and knocks them up in place, where your follow-up Vault Breaker and armor shred help your team finish the target. Do not gamble on the lock when a cleaner angle is one rotation away, and never spend it on the frontline tank you were not going to kill anyway. If the enemy clusters, a charged Q into the pack still buys a knockup, and your shield keeps you alive through the dive. The whole fight comes down to picking the right person to remove and committing fully; choose well and it is four against five before anyone else uses a spell.

Caitlyn out-ranges your feather setup and traps the ground your feathers need to occupy, so the lane phase is hers. In teamfights your root and self-peel out-value her single-target siege.
Ashe's constant slows stop you from spacing your feather placements, her Volley out-pokes your laning, and her arrow punishes the moment you step up. A slowed Xayah cannot reposition to fire back.

gamePlan.overview:
Xayah controls the Dragon lane with the feathers she leaves on the ground. Each ability cast loads three Clean Cuts stacks, up to five, and following attacks consume them to pierce through enemies and plant a feather at maximum range. Double Daggers plants two directly, while Featherstorm plants five. Bladecaller recalls every planted feather globally; an enemy must be hit by at least three returning feathers to be rooted, and repeated feathers deal progressively reduced damage to that target.

Her game is positioning and patience. Featherstorm makes Xayah untargetable for 1.5 seconds and lets her move, but she cannot attack or cast during it. When she lands, the five newly planted feathers create a strong immediate Bladecaller angle; reposition during the airborne window so their return path crosses the diver or clustered backline.

The costs are a weak early game, fragility to burst, and needing her feathers placed before the fight rather than during it.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Place feathers patiently. Drop them through your trades and waveclear, and only pull the root when the blades line up through the enemy carry; a rushed callback roots minions and nothing else. You are fragile early, so farm safely, lean on your support to set up root angles, and hold your ultimate as the answer to ganks and all-ins. The lane is about building good feather positions, not brawling before you are ready.
gamePlan.midGame: Items make the feather root deadly. Your root plus a support engage turns Dragon skirmishes into picks, and your sustained area damage punishes enemies who bunch up. Featherstorm lets you avoid a decisive engage while moving to reshape the feather angle. Xayah cannot keep attacking or casting during it, so the payoff comes after landing: recall its five feathers with Bladecaller to damage and root anyone crossed by at least three.
gamePlan.lateGame: You are a teamfight carry who peels for herself. Scatter feathers as the fight develops, pull them through clustered enemies, and hold Featherstorm for a committed dive or lethal spell. Move during its untargetability to put the five new feathers on the far side of your attacker, then cast Bladecaller after landing for the root. The ultimate buys time and movement, but it is not a dash and does not make flanks harmless.
gamePlan.teamfights: Place the feathers, then pull the root through the fight. Plant them during the opening exchanges, then call them back when at least three return paths cross the targets that matter. Hold Featherstorm for the moment a dive or lethal ability commits: become untargetable, move to a safer point, let its five feathers land, then immediately evaluate the Bladecaller root. You are both the area-damage carry and your own peel, so pick an angle that lets the feathers do both.

gamePlan.overview:
Zeri is a mobile marksman whose basic attack fires Burst Fire rounds. Electrocute zaps a target area for magic damage and a decaying slow; killing an enemy with it refunds all of its mana cost and half its remaining cooldown, making it a precise farming tool. Ultrashock Laser is a physical-damage pulse stopped by the first enemy, but striking terrain creates a delayed laser line after 0.85 seconds that grants sight and critically strikes against champions and monsters.

Spark Surge dashes a short distance or rides much farther when cast beside terrain. It then empowers Zeri's next three attacks to pierce, with modified damage after the first target and bonus magic damage to the first enemy hit. Champion attacks reduce its remaining cooldown, with critical strikes granting the larger refund. Zeri can cast Ultrashock Laser and Lightning Crash during the dash, enabling a terrain ride into a delayed wall laser or ultimate nova.

The costs are sharp: short range, a squishy frame, and a famously weak early game where her low chip damage leaves her exploitable. She wins by surviving to the items and terrain where her mobility takes over.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Survive the weak early phase. Use Electrocute to last-hit when its full mana refund and partial cooldown refund are available, and line Ultrashock Laser into terrain when the delayed beam can reach through the wave. Preserve Spark Surge for a safe terrain ride unless its three empowered piercing attacks clearly win the trade. Respect crowd control and remember that the long wall ride depends on casting beside terrain.
gamePlan.midGame: Clear the Dragon-lane wave before rotating and fight near terrain that offers Spark Surge an escape without separating Zeri from allied peel. Basic attacks against champions reduce the dash cooldown, with critical attacks reducing it further. Lightning Crash starts Overcharge only if the initial nova hits a champion; later champion hits extend the state and build short-lived movement-speed stacks. Arrive before dragon or Herald so the first dash and wall angle are chosen before the enemy engage begins.
gamePlan.lateGame: Push the side wave only when Zeri can rejoin before Baron or Elder is contested. Cast Lightning Crash where the initial nova will hit a champion, then keep safe champion contact so Overcharge and its movement stacks continue. Fight near a wall that creates a useful Spark Surge exit, but remain close enough to allied peel that an enemy dash cannot isolate you after the ride. Overcharged Burst Fire chains reduced damage through nearby visible enemies, so attack the closest safe target rather than forcing access to the backline.
gamePlan.teamfights: Keep moving without wasting the wall ride. Basic attacks against champions refund Spark Surge, and its next three attacks pierce after the dash. Cast Ultrashock Laser during a terrain ride when the wall angle will create its delayed line, and use Lightning Crash during the dash only when the nova will actually hit a champion and activate Overcharge. The chain lightning rewards continued champion contact, but one missed reset window can still end the momentum.

gamePlan.overview:
Zyra is a control mage who fights through her plants. Deadly Spines bursts at a target location after a short delay and spawns a Thorn Spitter beneath each enemy champion, large monster, or epic monster it hits. Grasping Roots travels through enemies, roots them, and spawns one plant beneath the first champion hit; or at maximum range if it hits no champion. Rampant Growth enrages nearby existing plants, while Stranglethorns is a delayed ground area that damages, later knocks up, spawns plants beneath hit champions and large monsters, and enrages the plants it touches.

You win by poking and zoning, then scaling into teamfights. She is not a roam-snowball mid or a flank assassin; she owns a slice of the map with plants and makes standing in it expensive. Land Deadly Spines on champions or large monsters and aim Grasping Roots so its guaranteed endpoint plant appears where it can fire, then enrage the patch and let the thorns chip enemies off waves and objectives.

The catch is obvious. She is extremely squishy with no dash and no blink, and her damage leans on plants an enemy can walk up and destroy before they fire. Spend the snare wrong, or get caught on cooldown, and an immobile mage with nothing left is exactly the target every assassin in the lobby drafted for.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Play the early lane around plant placement. Deadly Spines only spawns a plant when it hits a champion or large monster, while Grasping Roots creates one under its first champion hit or at maximum range, so aim each cast with the resulting Thorn Spitter in mind. Your strongest early pattern is the root into a fresh plant: it pins them in place while the plant attacks. Watch your mana closely, because an empty Zyra is a squishy mage with no plants and nowhere to go.
gamePlan.midGame: Clear the mid wave before moving to river, then use plants and Grasping Roots to control the entrance your team wants to hold. A root on the enemy jungler can create time to start dragon or Herald, but check lane priority and allied damage before committing to the pit. When no objective is active, move through established vision and cast from fog at an overextended side laner. If the river is dark and the enemy assassin is missing, stay with your jungler instead of checking an angle alone.
gamePlan.lateGame: Clear distant waves only when you can return before Baron or Elder is threatened. During setup, position behind your frontline and place plants across a choke the enemy must cross. Hold Grasping Roots when a diver is missing, then use it to peel before layering Stranglethorns on the committed enemies. Move with teammates while establishing vision, because Zyra cannot safely check a brush after spending her control.
gamePlan.teamfights: Open with Grasping Roots when it catches a target your team can reach, then place Stranglethorns where the enemy must either separate or remain for the delayed knockup. Spawn plants with Deadly Spines and Roots as the fight begins, then use Rampant Growth when several plants can attack useful targets. If an assassin is threatening the backline, keep the root and ultimate for peel instead of forcing the first cast onto the enemy frontline.

Lulu is a pure enchanter with no engage and no poke to answer yours, so she spends the lane shielding while your plants chip her duo. The early game belongs to the one doing the punishing.
You throw five threats for every answer she owns: plants chip her constantly, your root trades even with her binding, and Black Shield blocks one spell out of a rotation that never stops coming.

gamePlan.overview:
Zyra is a support built around damage and zone control. Her damaging abilities automatically spawn Thorn Spitters under specific hit targets or at Grasping Roots' endpoint, so she creates plants by landing spells rather than planting hidden seeds. Stranglethorns damages a large ground area, spawns more plants under hit champions and large monsters, enrages plants it touches, and knocks enemies up after two seconds.

In the 2v2 she plays a poke-and-zone game that punishes anyone who has to walk toward her. Land Deadly Spines on a champion to spawn a plant beneath them, or send Grasping Roots through the wave so it roots the carry and creates a Thorn Spitter beneath the first champion hit. A duo that respects your zone gives up the wave; a duo that ignores it gives up health.

The catch is her durability. Zyra is fragile and immobile, so a hook or assassin can punish her after Grasping Roots and Stranglethorns are spent. Zone from the edge of her range, keep the root available when a diver is missing, and position near allied peel rather than beside the frontline.
gamePlan.earlyGame: Play from behind the range where your spawned plants will fire. Land Deadly Spines on a champion for its plant, then fire Grasping Roots through the wave so it catches the enemy carry and creates another Thorn Spitter under the first champion hit. Your poke out-damages many Dragon lane duos, but keep Grasping Roots available when a dive is coming and ward the river so the enemy jungler never finds your immobile frame unseen.
gamePlan.midGame: Your roam threat is real now, because a rooted target a lane over is a dead target. Use Grasping Roots and Deadly Spines to establish plants around mid or river before objectives. Around dragon and Herald, control the entrances and hold Stranglethorns for the moment both teams clump at the contest; it spawns and enrages plants while threatening the delayed knockup.
gamePlan.lateGame: One ultimate can decide the game, and one bad position can decide it the other way. Late game, cast into chokes to establish Thorn Spitters on the ground the enemy must cross, and wait for their team to stack up before Stranglethorns launches them. Stand at the edge of the fight and treat Grasping Roots as both opener and self-defense.
gamePlan.teamfights: You are the area-denial support, so fight from the back and let the plants do the frontline work. Establish Thorn Spitters by landing Deadly Spines or Grasping Roots before bodies collide, then use Rampant Growth to enrage the plants already present. When their team stacks to dive or contest an objective, cast Stranglethorns across the clump so its delayed knockup lands during your team's follow-up. Keep the root as peel if a diver slips through, because it is the only thing that can save you or your carry.
